## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}
\end{marginfigure}

_When is another token, candidate, check, or model call worth its cost?_

A bounded model call returns a candidate, but a difficult task may justify more work before the runtime selects a result. Longer reasoning can resolve implications of information already available; alternative candidates can expose a better solution; a check can reveal a defect and guide revision. These choices spend different amounts of time and resources, and their value depends on the task and the method used to select the final output. A larger candidate pool helps only when useful alternatives survive selection, while a high check score supplies a judgment whose relevance depends on the check's scope and reliability. The engineering problem is to allocate deliberation under explicit limits and determine whether the resulting gain justifies its cost. Candidate plans also depend on observations that can become stale, so revision must preserve valid work without carrying invalid assumptions forward. In H·S·A terms, deliberation consumes resources and can extend the horizon through additional model turns and governed tool interactions; it does not expand the agent's authority or turn a proposal into an accepted result. A bounded policy must therefore specify how it generates, selects, checks, and stops, including what happens when its budget ends without sufficient acceptance evidence.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain how additional reasoning, alternative candidates, and new observations can each improve a bounded model decision.
- Compare depth, breadth, and feedback by their resource use and sequential dependencies.
- Distinguish candidate availability from selected-output quality when evaluating voting, learned scoring, and task-specific checks.
- Calculate accepted-set precision from stated checker error rates and explain how adaptive search can change those assumptions.
- Represent a candidate plan as a dependency graph and identify which parts require revision after an observation changes.
- Design stopping rules that enforce resource ceilings without treating budget exhaustion as acceptance evidence.
- Evaluate deliberation policies under common budgets and permissions, including actual spend, output quality, abstentions, and deadline effects.

:::

## When One Response Is Insufficient {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-insufficient-response}

The repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) has inspected the connection-pool implementation, but the first patch still rests on an uncertain diagnosis. Requests occasionally wait after a connection becomes available. One explanation is an overly short timeout; another is a missed notification when a worker returns a connection. The model proposes increasing the timeout. That is a plausible candidate, not evidence that the timeout caused the failure. Applying it immediately could hide the symptom while leaving the synchronization defect intact.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_h.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the Horizon axis highlighted."}

*Deliberation extends the horizon with extra model turns and checks inside one decision, and hard ceilings bound that spend.*
:::

The runtime has several ways to spend additional work before choosing a patch. It can permit a longer derivation of the locking sequence, request alternatives that change different parts of the implementation, or run a targeted test that records whether a waiting worker receives the return notification. These choices buy different things. More reasoning can expose a contradiction in the supplied source. Another sample can discover an approach absent from the first candidate. An instrumented test can provide an observation about an execution that neither candidate has observed.

The distinction is between computation and observation. Extra computation improves an answer using information already present; within one generation the model can revise an earlier conclusion even though the earlier text remains in its prefix. Only an executed test reports what the program does, and its result supports exactly the property and conditions that the test exercised.

Suppose the targeted test controls the ordering of a waiting worker and a returning connection. Its trace shows the connection becoming available while the waiter remains blocked past the notification point. This observation directs attention toward the notification path, and the agent uses it to construct and check a revised candidate; neither diagnosis is permission to modify a production service. @Fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree sets this sequence beside the alternative of carrying the first explanation straight into a patch.

::: {#fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Committing to a Hypothesis versus Checking It**: Both paths start from the same connection-pool failure. On the left, generation builds on the timeout explanation without any observation that separates it from a missed notification, so the patch can hide the symptom while the defect remains. On the right, a targeted test orders a waiting worker and a returning connection, and its observation contradicts the timeout explanation before any edit. The revised candidate passes the reproducer, which still falls short of task acceptance." fig-alt="Two columns below a box stating that a request waits after a connection becomes available. Left column, labeled commit to the first hypothesis: one hypothesis that the timeout is too short, generation that builds on it with no new evidence, and a timeout patch applied unchecked, ending in a box reading symptom masked, notification defect remains. Right column, labeled check before committing: two hypotheses held, timeout too short and missed notification, a targeted test that orders a blocked waiter and a returning connection and observes the waiter still blocked, and a revised candidate that notifies a waiter on return, ending in a box reading reproducer passes, acceptance still pending. A dashed arrow labeled contradicts H1 runs from the test to the left column."}
![](images/svg/diagnostic_tree.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-probe-allocation
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PROBE AND GENERATION ALLOWANCES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-probe-versus-generation.
# │ Goal: Compare a short diagnostic operation with an output allowance.
# │ Show: Generation time and output charge, distinct from probe duration.
# │ How: Reuse the registry weight-read allowance from Foundation Model;
# │      exclude prefill, queueing, transport, and probe setup overhead.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8

class ProbeAllocation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    answer_tokens = 1_024  # hypothetical output length
    probe_time = 0.040 * second  # hypothetical already-prepared test duration
    output_price = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical dollars per output token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    answer_time = answer_tokens * token_time
    answer_cost = answer_tokens * output_price
    time_ratio = answer_time / probe_time

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(answer_time > probe_time > 0 * second, "Positive scenario durations")
    check(answer_cost > 0 * USD, "Output has a positive scenario charge")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    answer_tokens_str = fmt_int(answer_tokens)
    probe_time_str = fmt_time(probe_time, unit="ms", precision=0)
    token_time_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit="ms", precision=2)
    answer_time_str = fmt_time(answer_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    answer_cost_str = fmt_usd(answer_cost, precision=5)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_price * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    time_mult_str = fmt_multiple(time_ratio, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-03-probe-versus-generation .callout-notebook title="A probe versus a longer answer"}

**Problem**: A prepared diagnostic test takes `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str`. A proposed explanation contains `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str` output tokens. How long does the explanation take to generate relative to the test?

**Variables**: The illustrative output allowance from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost is `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` per token, a registry-derived estimate rather than a measured service rate. The hypothetical output price is `{python} ProbeAllocation.output_price_str` per million tokens. Prompt processing, queueing, transport, test preparation, and the later call that reads the observation are excluded.

**Math**: `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str` tokens at `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` each take `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str` and cost `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_cost_str` in output charges. Dividing by the test's `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str` gives `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: When the open question is what the program does, an observation is two to three orders of magnitude cheaper in time than more generation. The probe wins whenever its preparation plus run time stays below the explanation's `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str` and its outcome separates the competing hypotheses; a test that cannot reproduce the fault buys nothing at any price. Spend on the operation that resolves the current uncertainty.

:::

Test-time compute extends the bounded-call contract. The runtime allocates extra generation and checks, keeps a completed response distinct from a completed repair, and specifies both how much work is permitted and whether that work extends one candidate, explores alternatives, or conditions a revision on observations.

## Three Compute Allocation Axes {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-computation-allocation}

For the connection-pool repair, a longer explanation, several alternative patches, and a generate–test–revise loop can consume similar output budgets while producing different dependencies. The explanation must finish its sequential generation. Independent alternatives may run concurrently. A revision that uses a test result must wait for that result. These dependencies determine which work belongs on the critical path and which state must remain available.

**Depth**\index{Depth axis!definition} extends computation within a candidate, **breadth**\index{Breadth axis!definition} explores multiple candidates, and **feedback**\index{Feedback axis!definition} supplies observations to a later revision. A **test-time deliberation rollout**\index{Test-time deliberation rollout!definition}\index{Deliberation!rollout definition} is one bounded candidate-generation path, possibly including checks and observation-conditioned revisions. A policy can combine the axes, for example by generating several candidates, checking each, and extending only a promising one. The model's weights remain fixed during this work, and every axis draws on one allowance.

::: {#dfn-vol3-test-time-compute-budget .callout-definition title="Test-time compute budget"}

***Test-time compute budget***\index{Test-time compute budget!definition} is the per-decision allowance of processed and generated tokens, model calls, checks, and elapsed time that a runtime may spend, with the model's weights fixed, before it must select a candidate, abstain, or escalate.

1.  **Significance**: The budget sets the attempt cost in the cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}} = \mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]/p_{\text{acc}}$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task), and deliberation earns its place only when it raises $p_{\text{acc}}$ faster than it raises the attempt cost.
2.  **Distinction**: Training compute changes the weights once for every future task; test-time compute is spent again on every decision, and a model's internal reasoning allowance is only one of its control surfaces beside external calls and checks.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the ceiling as the expected spend, or treating an exhausted budget as evidence that the best remaining candidate is acceptable.

:::

@Fig-vol3-allocation-axes separates these dependencies before assigning them a resource budget.

::: {#fig-vol3-allocation-axes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Three compute allocation topologies**: Depth extends one candidate; breadth exposes separate sampled candidate paths followed by selection; feedback makes a later candidate depend on an observed check result. The arrows show dependencies, not guaranteed latency, cost, or correctness." fig-alt="Three panels labeled Depth, Breadth, and Feedback. Depth connects an input through two reasoning segments to a candidate. Breadth branches an input into three sample streams that converge on a selector. Feedback connects a candidate to a governed check or tool, then an observation, then a revised candidate."}
![](images/svg/three_compute_allocation_axes.svg)
:::

### Sequential extension along the depth axis

Depth allows a model to generate intermediate steps before returning its final proposal. For the repair, those steps might trace lock acquisition, connection return, and waiter notification through the supplied source. Later generated tokens can use the earlier derivation to identify an inconsistent assumption or construct a different proposal. The benefit comes from additional computation over the available information, not from changing the underlying model.

Generation still follows the conditional process established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive. Extending one response lengthens a dependent sequence, so its generation time grows about linearly with the added tokens under a fixed serving configuration (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}). A longer trace is evidence of more computation, not of a patch having run. The runtime must also reserve enough of the call's output budget for a complete usable candidate; exhausting that budget leaves the invocation subject to the same status-first handling as any other call.

### Parallel sampling along the breadth axis

Breadth spends work on alternative candidates. The runtime might request several repairs from the same source excerpt and task description, using the sampling controls of @sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive. Conditional on a fixed request and independent random draws, these samples can be statistically independent while still sharing a systematic limitation, such as assigning little probability to a correct notification protocol. Independent draws can all miss the useful alternative.

Separate candidates need not wait for one another, so breadth exposes concurrency. Concurrency is cheap in latency because of how decoding uses the accelerator. At small batch sizes, each decode step is dominated by reading the model weights, so memory bandwidth sets a floor on step time (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}). A batch of $N$ streams reads those weights once per step for all of them. Spending $N$ candidates' worth of tokens along the depth axis therefore multiplies the generation path by about $N$, while spending them across $N$ concurrent streams leaves it near the duration of the longest candidate. The advantage holds only while the batch remains bound by weight reads and fits in memory.

Memory is where breadth pays. Each stream keeps its own key-value (KV) cache for the tokens it has generated, so the retained state grows as

$$
M_{\text{KV}}^{\text{breadth}} \propto P + \sum_{n=1}^{N} K_n
$$

when the $P$-token prompt is stored once and shared, and as $NP + \sum_n K_n$ when it is not. @Sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree develops how a service shares such prefixes. When the combined state exceeds capacity, the service must run candidates in waves, and the breadth path degrades from the longest candidate toward the sum of all of them. With resource contention, individual durations can also increase. Whether identical prompts share processing or earn a billing discount depends on the service.

Breadth also produces more candidates to retain and assess, and it pays only when the system can choose among them or use their differences to guide further work. A pool that contains a good patch still needs a selector that finds it, so selection is part of the compute policy, not a free final step.

### Observation-conditioned revision along the feedback axis

Feedback changes the next request using observations from a check or other permitted operation. The repair agent generates a patch, the runtime arranges a bounded test, and the next call receives a diagnostic such as the blocked waiter's trace. The observation constrains the next candidate more directly than a request to produce a different explanation of the same input.

The check reports failure, passage, or an inconclusive outcome. Failure can identify a specific defect; passage supports the covered property under the exercised conditions; the task's acceptance decision remains a separate step. Diagnostic execution is a real action: it consumes resources, stays within the task's permissions, and has real effects even when it serves deliberation.

Feedback adds dependencies: a revision cannot use a result that has not arrived. If the runtime retains every earlier proposal and observation in the next request, input length also grows. With initial input length $P_1$, candidate lengths $K_j$, and observation lengths $|O_j|$, this append-only policy gives

$$P_r = P_1 + \sum_{j=1}^{r-1}(K_j + |O_j|)$$

The equation describes one context policy. Sending shorter observations or dropping obsolete proposals lowers the cost and also changes what the revision can see, a choice @sec-vol3-context-engineering develops; the allocation policy counts the representation it actually sends.

### Comparing allocations under one output ceiling

The three axes can now be compared on the quantities a runtime schedules against. Let $t_{\text{prefill}}(P)$ be the time to process a $P$-token input, $t_{\text{step}}$ the time per generated token, $T_{\text{decode}}(K)$ the time to generate $K$ tokens, and $t_{\text{check},r}$ the duration of the check in feedback round $r$. With $K_{\text{ext}}$ tokens of extended depth, $N$ breadth candidates run concurrently, and $R$ feedback rounds, the critical paths are

$$
\begin{aligned}
T^{\text{depth}} &\approx t_{\text{prefill}}(P) + K_{\text{ext}}\,t_{\text{step}},\\
T^{\text{breadth}} &\approx t_{\text{prefill}}(P) + \max_{n} T_{\text{decode}}(K_n),\\
T^{\text{feedback}} &\approx \sum_{r=1}^{R}\bigl(t_{\text{prefill}}(P_r) + T_{\text{decode}}(K_r) + t_{\text{check},r}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path}

The breadth expression assumes capacity for all $N$ streams at an unchanged step time; without it, the maximum drifts toward a sum over waves. The feedback expression grows twice, once through its sequential checks and once through the lengthening inputs $P_r$. @Tbl-vol3-allocation-model sets the paths of @eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path beside the work each axis processes, the model state it must retain, and the source of any new information.

| **Axis** | **Tokens processed**                      | **Critical path**                   | **Peak retained model state**                   | **New information**                      |
|:---------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Depth    | $P + K_{\text{ext}}$                      | One dependent sequence              | One context of $P + K_{\text{ext}}$ tokens      | None beyond the request and weights      |
| Breadth  | $P + \sum_n K_n$ (prompt shared)          | Longest candidate, given capacity   | $N$ contexts, $P + \sum_n K_n$ tokens if shared | Sampling variation over the same request |
| Feedback | $\sum_{r}(P_r + K_r)$, with $P_r$ growing | Sum of rounds, including each check | One active context of $P_R + K_R$ tokens        | Observations from executed checks        |

: **Resource model of the three allocation axes**: Symbolic accounting of processed tokens, critical path, retained model state, and information source. Concurrency and prefix sharing are capacity and implementation assumptions, not properties of the axis. {#tbl-vol3-allocation-model tbl-colwidths="[11,23,22,25,19]"}

Only the feedback row admits information the model did not already have. The notebook below evaluates these expressions for one repair with prefill omitted, showing how equal output ceilings produce unequal work.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-allocation-axes
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMMON OUTPUT CEILING, DIFFERENT EXECUTION TOPOLOGIES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-matched-budget-axes.
# │ Goal: Separate output ceilings, actual spend, and dependent elapsed time.
# │ Show: Input/output counts, hypothetical bills, and generation/check time.
# │ How: Hold model allowance fixed; stipulate four concurrent breadth streams.
# │      Feedback appends each prior candidate and report; no cache discounts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8

class AllocationAxes:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    prompt = 4_096  # hypothetical fully serialized initial input tokens
    ceiling = 4_096  # common total generated-token ceiling
    candidates = 4  # breadth concurrency and candidate count
    candidate_tokens = 1_024  # hypothetical generated length per short candidate
    rounds = 3  # hypothetical feedback rounds actually used
    report = 340  # tokens appended per complete observation
    check_time = 1.5 * second  # hypothetical duration per feedback check
    price_in = 3 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-input-token price
    price_out = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-output-token price

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    depth_input = prompt
    depth_output = ceiling
    breadth_input = candidates * prompt
    breadth_output = candidates * candidate_tokens
    feedback_input = rounds * prompt + (candidate_tokens + report) * rounds * (rounds - 1) // 2
    feedback_output = rounds * candidate_tokens
    depth_time = depth_output * token_time
    breadth_time = candidate_tokens * token_time
    feedback_time = rounds * (candidate_tokens * token_time + check_time)
    depth_cost = depth_input * price_in + depth_output * price_out
    breadth_cost = breadth_input * price_in + breadth_output * price_out
    feedback_cost = feedback_input * price_in + feedback_output * price_out
    path_ratio = (depth_time / breadth_time).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    bill_ratio = (breadth_cost / depth_cost).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    breadth_premium = breadth_input - depth_input  # (N - 1) P re-read prompt tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(depth_output == breadth_output == ceiling, "Depth and breadth exhaust ceiling")
    check(feedback_output < ceiling, "Feedback uses less than the output ceiling")
    check(feedback_input == 16_380, "Append-only feedback input accounting")
    check(depth_time > feedback_time > breadth_time, "Scenario critical-path ordering")
    check(breadth_premium == (candidates - 1) * prompt, "Breadth premium is the re-read prompt")
    check(bill_ratio > 1 and path_ratio > 1, "Breadth buys path length with bill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    ceiling_str = fmt_int(ceiling)
    candidates_str = fmt_int(candidates)
    candidate_tokens_str = fmt_int(candidate_tokens)
    rounds_str = fmt_int(rounds)
    report_str = fmt_int(report)
    check_time_str = fmt_time(check_time, unit="s", precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    depth_input_str = fmt_int(depth_input)
    depth_output_str = fmt_int(depth_output)
    breadth_input_str = fmt_int(breadth_input)
    breadth_output_str = fmt_int(breadth_output)
    feedback_input_str = fmt_int(feedback_input)
    feedback_output_str = fmt_int(feedback_output)
    depth_time_str = fmt_time(depth_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    breadth_time_str = fmt_time(breadth_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    feedback_time_str = fmt_time(feedback_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    depth_cost_str = fmt_usd(depth_cost, precision=5)
    breadth_cost_str = fmt_usd(breadth_cost, precision=5)
    feedback_cost_str = fmt_usd(feedback_cost, precision=5)
    path_mult_str = fmt_multiple(path_ratio, precision=0)
    bill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bill_ratio, precision=1)
    breadth_premium_str = fmt_int(breadth_premium)
```

::: {#nbk-03-matched-budget-axes .callout-notebook title="One decision, three allocations"}

**Problem**: A repair request starts with `{python} AllocationAxes.prompt_str` input tokens and a common ceiling of `{python} AllocationAxes.ceiling_str` generated tokens. How do depth, breadth, and feedback spend that allowance?

**Variables**: Reuse the illustrative per-token allowance from the preceding example. Breadth has capacity for `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` concurrent streams at that same rate. Each short candidate uses `{python} AllocationAxes.candidate_tokens_str` generated tokens. Feedback uses `{python} AllocationAxes.rounds_str` rounds, each followed by a `{python} AllocationAxes.check_time_str` check returning `{python} AllocationAxes.report_str` tokens. Later feedback requests append earlier candidates and reports. Hypothetical prices are `{python} AllocationAxes.price_in_str` per million input tokens and `{python} AllocationAxes.price_out_str` per million output tokens, without cache discounts. Generation allowances omit prefill, queueing, and transport; the feedback allowance additionally includes its checks. The bill counts model tokens only.

| Allocation |                                 Input tokens |                                 Output tokens |              Generation and included checks |                            Model-token bill |
|:-----------|---------------------------------------------:|----------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|
| Depth      |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_input_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_output_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_time_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_cost_str` |
| Breadth    |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_input_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_output_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_time_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_cost_str` |
| Feedback   | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_input_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_output_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_time_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_cost_str` |
: **Allocation accounting under a common output ceiling**: Equal ceilings produce unequal spend. Allowances omit prefill, queueing, selection, and tool charges. {#tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs}

**Math**: In @tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs, depth generates all `{python} AllocationAxes.ceiling_str` tokens on one path; breadth generates `{python} AllocationAxes.candidate_tokens_str` on each of `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` concurrent paths, so its path is `{python} AllocationAxes.path_mult_str` shorter, while reading the prompt `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` times adds `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_premium_str` input tokens and makes its bill `{python} AllocationAxes.bill_mult_str` that of depth. Feedback's input over $R$ rounds is $RP + (K+|O|)\,R(R-1)/2$, or `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_input_str` tokens at $R$ = `{python} AllocationAxes.rounds_str`, because each round re-reads every earlier candidate and report.

**Systems insight**: Breadth trades bill for path length, and the entire premium is the $(N-1)P$ re-read prompt. The knob is the prompt-to-output ratio: a long repository context makes breadth's premium grow linearly with both $N$ and $P$, while a short prompt or a shared prefix (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree) removes most of it. Feedback lands between the other two on time and bill and is the only row that buys new information. No success rates enter this arithmetic, so it ranks resources, not quality.

:::

### Internal budgets and external orchestration {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-latent-vs-scaffold}

A model service may expose an internal reasoning allowance, while the runtime can independently choose how many calls to make and which observations to supply. These are different control surfaces. An internal allowance changes the work permitted within a call; external orchestration chooses candidate branches, invokes checks, and constructs subsequent requests. Depending on the interface, intermediate generation may be hidden or only partly exposed. The runtime must use reported usage and invocation status rather than infer the work from the visible answer's length.

### Reasoning models and generation allowances {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-reasoning-models}

**Reasoning models**\index{Reasoning model!definition} are trained with reinforcement learning on tasks whose answers can be checked, such as mathematics with known answers and code with tests. They learn to produce long intermediate traces that propose, check, and backtrack within one generation [@openai2024o1; @deepseekai2025deepseekr1]. Three consequences follow for the runtime. Reasoning tokens are output tokens, generated and metered like any other whether or not the interface displays them. A reasoning-budget field on the call makes depth a per-call allocation that the runtime controls rather than a fixed property of the model. Trained reasoning still draws only on the request and the weights. The model can recheck arithmetic inside its trace, but it cannot observe whether a patch passes a test it never ran.

Models trained this way use an internal allowance differently from models trained primarily for short responses, so budget calibration is model-specific. Because the trace may be hidden, the runtime's own candidate and check records are what it can inspect, and they support diagnosis of the policy rather than proof of the candidate.

Because depth is a per-call budget, the runtime can allocate it task by task, and the useful question becomes what each kind of spending buys on problems of different difficulty.

::: {#exmp-03-compute-optimal-allocation .callout-example title="Compute-optimal test-time allocation"}

**Scenario**: @snell2024scaling compared ways of spending a fixed test-time budget, from sequential revision of one candidate to parallel sampling and search guided by a learned scorer of intermediate steps (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification), on problems binned by how hard they were for the base model.

**Diagnosis**: On easier problems, sequential revision made the better use of the budget. On harder problems, a mix that added parallel exploration or search did better. On the hardest problems, neither approach produced much gain. In a comparison matched on total FLOPs, a compute-optimal allocation let a smaller model outperform a model 14 times larger, but only on problems where the smaller model already had a non-trivial success rate; on the hardest problems, spending the same FLOPs on the larger model was more effective.

**Systems lesson**: Test-time compute multiplies an existing success rate rather than creating one. Route budget by estimated difficulty, and send tasks whose base success is near zero to a stronger model or to escalation instead of to more samples.

:::

A runtime cannot observe difficulty directly, so it approximates this allocation with cheap signals obtained before committing a large budget: whether two or three short samples agree, whether a fast static check passes, and how earlier tasks of the same class fared. Decisions whose signals agree receive a small allowance and one candidate. Decisions whose signals disagree receive a larger allowance or a search. Decisions still unresolved after a bounded spend are escalated rather than given more tokens. Each signal is a proxy for difficulty, and its value for routing must be measured on held-out tasks like any other predictor.

Internal reasoning and external search combine. A candidate may receive enough depth to express a coherent repair, then compete with alternatives or undergo a targeted test. Long tool delays lengthen feedback's critical path, and weak checks shrink the information feedback contributes, so the allocation is a measured policy choice per task class. The check a runtime uses to accept candidates at test time is also the kind of signal that reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards trains against. A check good enough to gate a commit here is a candidate reward in @sec-vol3-rlvr, and its blind spots carry over to training.

::: {#chk-03-compute-allocation-axes .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing an allocation"}

- [ ] **Information**: For the connection-pool repair, which axis can separate a short timeout from a missed notification, and why can the other two not?
- [ ] **Concurrency**: If the service admits only one candidate at a time, how long does the notebook's breadth allocation take to generate, and which allocation then has the shortest path?
- [ ] **Breadth premium**: How many extra input tokens does `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str`-way breadth read compared with depth for a `{python} AllocationAxes.prompt_str`-token prompt, and what happens to that premium when the repository context grows eightfold?
- [ ] **Evidence**: If a revised patch passes a targeted test, what additional information determines whether the task may stop?

:::

Depth, breadth, and feedback specify where extra work goes, but none specifies which candidate should survive. Even an allocation that produces a useful repair can fail if the selector favors a plausible incorrect alternative. The next decision is therefore how to compare candidates while accounting for the cost and limitations of the evidence used to choose them.

## Candidate Selection {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity}

Breadth gives the agent a set of proposals, not a better answer by itself. In the connection-pool repair task, one candidate might increase a timeout, another might add retries, and another might change how the connection-return path notifies waiting callers. The runtime must decide which proposal, if any, has enough supporting evidence to return. That decision consumes part of the same budget that produced the candidates.

Two questions separate the generation policy from the selection policy: whether the candidate pool contains a solution that meets the task's criteria, and whether the selector can identify such a candidate without accepting an unsuitable one. A generation policy can improve the first quantity while leaving the second unchanged. Conversely, a better selector can improve the delivered result without generating any additional candidates.

### Useful variation among candidates

Different strings need not represent different approaches. Renaming variables or rewriting a loop can leave the same faulty notification handling intact. For the repair task, alternatives are useful when they explore plausible causes or repairs that the available checks can distinguish. A change to the notification path and a longer timeout test different hypotheses; several differently worded explanations of the same timeout change may add little.

This limitation differs from statistical dependence. With the task, prompt, model, and sampling policy fixed, separate generations using independent random draws are independent and identically distributed even when the model often repeats the same mistake: if nearly all probability mass favors timeout changes, independent sampling mostly produces timeout changes.

Across a collection of tasks, shared limitations still matter. A model may solve familiar tasks frequently and unfamiliar tasks rarely. Repeated attempts on the same difficult task then fail together more often than an analysis using the average success rate across all tasks would predict. Independence conditional on a fixed task does not justify treating every attempt across a mixed workload as a draw with one common success probability. Feedback-conditioned generation changes the distribution again: later candidates depend on what earlier checks revealed.

The runtime can change sampling settings or ask candidates to investigate different plausible hypotheses while preserving the original requirements. More variation can also introduce irrelevant approaches, malformed outputs, or violations of constraints that every solution must satisfy, so the test of a diversification technique is whether it improves the delivered result under the same resource limits.

Structural and behavioral comparisons remove redundant work. Normalizing variable names identifies some superficial code differences; running candidates against the same test inputs reveals repeated observed behavior. Each establishes a bounded relation, syntactic equivalence under the normalization or agreement on those tests, and deduplication is sound when that relation preserves the property being evaluated.

### Choosing a selection policy

A selector may use direct checks, answer agreement, learned ranking, or a combination. The task and the available evidence determine which apply; they are alternatives, not fixed stages of one pipeline.

Direct checks compare a candidate with explicit requirements. A parser can reject malformed code; a type checker can establish properties within its type system; a test harness can measure behavior on specified inputs. Each has its own scope: compiling says nothing about the notification bug, and a regression test covers the executions it runs. Candidate execution remains a governed action, so tests use the isolation and permissions appropriate to the task.

Answer agreement is useful when outputs have a meaningful comparison rule. **Self-consistency**\index{Self-consistency!definition} samples several reasoning paths and returns the most frequent final answer [@wang2022self]. For a numerical problem, the runtime normalizes the answer representation and takes the plurality. Agreement is evidence about the sampled distribution: several paths can reproduce the same misconception. For code repairs, textual voting is a poor comparison rule, agreement on observed behaviors carries the coverage limits just described, and a correct minority candidate deserves a direct check rather than a vote.

A learned ranker or model-based judge can compare candidates when direct checks cover only part of the task. It might score explanatory adequacy or prioritize patches for expensive testing. Its score remains an estimate whose relevance must be evaluated on the intended task distribution. Ranking asks which candidate looks better according to the scoring rule; acceptance asks whether there is sufficient evidence to return a candidate under the task's criteria. The highest score in a weak pool does not answer the acceptance question. A selector that answers it needs a check with a verdict, not a ranking.

::: {#dfn-vol3-verifier-guided-selection .callout-definition title="Verifier-guided selection"}

***Verifier-guided selection***\index{Verifier-guided selection!definition}\index{Verifier!definition} is a selection policy that returns a candidate only when a **verifier**, a check whose criteria and observations the candidate cannot modify, passes it, and abstains when no candidate passes.

1.  **Significance**: Its success rate is capped by pass@$k$, the chance the pool holds a passing candidate (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k), and the share of its selections that are correct is the verifier's precision on that pool; together they set $p_{\text{acc}}$ in the cost per accepted task.
2.  **Distinction**: Voting selects what the generator produces most often and learned ranking selects what a scorer prefers; only a verifier's verdict can justify returning a candidate instead of abstaining.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the verifier's pass as task acceptance; the verdict covers the checked property, and its false acceptance rate grows in importance as the pool's valid-candidate rate falls.

:::

The hypothetical repair pool in @tbl-vol3-candidate-diversity illustrates why these distinctions affect the result. The checks are deliberately incomplete: the reproducer exercises the known failure, while other workloads remain untested.

| **Candidate** | **Proposed repair**                                | **Observed check result**       | **Supported conclusion**                                  |
|:--------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| A             | Increase the timeout                               | Compiles; known failure remains | Structural validity is insufficient                       |
| B             | Retry after the timeout                            | Compiles; known failure remains | Different code can preserve the same defect               |
| C             | Change notification handling with malformed syntax | Parsing fails                   | This artifact cannot proceed to execution testing         |
| D             | Change notification handling with valid syntax     | Compiles; reproducer passes     | Promising repair, with untested behavior still unresolved |

: **Evidence for candidate selection**: A hypothetical repair pool separates the proposed mechanism, the observed result, and the conclusion each check supports. {#tbl-vol3-candidate-diversity tbl-colwidths="[12,25,30,33]"}

The runtime can compose checks according to their cost and their ability to eliminate unsuitable candidates. A relatively cheap structural check can save expensive execution or model-scoring work, but the ordering follows measured costs, not check categories. Tests can dominate latency, and a learned judge may need to read the prompt, the candidate, and supporting observations. Comparing all candidates jointly can have a different cost from scoring each independently. Selection therefore belongs in the deliberation budget from the start.

### Candidate availability under pass@$k$ {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k}

**pass@$k$**\index{Pass at k!definition} measures the probability that at least one of $k$ sampled candidates passes the specified tests [@chen2021evaluating]. It measures availability in the pool, not the success rate of the output a deployed selector returns.

For a fixed task and fixed generation policy, suppose independent samples each pass the tests with probability $p$. The probability that all $k$ samples fail is $(1-p)^k$, so

$$
\operatorname{pass@}k = 1-(1-p)^k.
$$

This expression is conditional on that task and sampling policy. To summarize a workload with different task-level pass probabilities, average the task-level quantities; substituting the workload's average $p$ generally gives a different result. For an adaptive policy that revises its prompt after feedback, evaluate the policy's resulting pools rather than assuming they follow this fixed-distribution formula.

In a benchmark, generate $n \ge k$ candidates for a task and let $c$ pass the fixed test criterion. Of the $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$, exactly $\binom{n-c}{k}$ contain only failures. The subset estimator is therefore

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{pass@}k}
= 1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},
$$

with the numerator taken as zero when $n-c<k$. Under independent, identically distributed sampling for the fixed task, this estimates the probability that a fresh pool of $k$ candidates contains a test-passing member without bias. Benchmark results average these estimates over tasks [@chen2021evaluating].

The relationship to deployed selection follows from the event being measured. If the selector must return an unchanged member of the same pool, it cannot return a test-passing candidate when the pool contains none. Its probability of returning a test-passing candidate is therefore at most pass@$k$, counting abstention as no returned pass. A selector that always finds a passing member whenever one exists reaches this ceiling; whether the deployed selector does, within the deployment's checking budget, is a separate measurement.

The predicate is passing these tests, which is narrower than satisfying the complete task requirements, and the ceiling covers only selectors that return an unchanged pool member; a selector that repairs candidates or synthesizes a new one generates additional artifacts. Report candidate availability alongside selected-output performance under the relevant criterion. @Sec-vol3-evaluation develops the broader distinction between a pool-level metric and reliability over repeated system runs.

Breadth has a price that pass@$k$ makes easy to compute. In **best-of-$N$ sampling**\index{Best-of-N sampling!definition}, the runtime generates $N$ candidates for one decision and returns one that its selector admits. The notebook below prices that pool against the simplest alternative, generating one candidate at a time and stopping at the first pass, under the most favorable selection assumption: the verifier is the acceptance check itself.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-best-of-n-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PRICE OF A LARGER POOL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price; fallacies (mixed-workload pass@N).
# │ Goal: Compare parallel best-of-N with stop-at-first-pass sequential retry
# │       at the same success probability.
# │ Show: pass@N, marginal gain of the last candidate, candidates per success.
# │ How: IID candidates for a fixed task; the verifier is the acceptance check;
# │      a perfect selector returns a passing member whenever one exists.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class BestOfN:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    p = 0.30  # hypothetical per-candidate pass probability for a fixed task
    pools = (1, 2, 4, 8)  # pool sizes compared
    p_easy = 0.60  # hypothetical mixed workload: half the tasks pass at this rate
    p_hard = 0.0  # hypothetical mixed workload: the other half never pass

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_max = pools[-1]
    pass_at = []
    for n in pools:
        pass_at.append(1 - (1 - p) ** n)
    pass_max = pass_at[-1]
    last_gain = p * (1 - p) ** (n_max - 1)
    parallel_per_success = n_max / pass_max
    seq_candidates = pass_max / p  # expected attempts, stop at first pass, cap n_max
    seq_per_success = seq_candidates / pass_max  # reduces to 1 / p
    cost_ratio = parallel_per_success / seq_per_success
    p_mix = (p_easy + p_hard) / 2
    naive_mix = 1 - (1 - p_mix) ** n_max
    true_mix = ((1 - (1 - p_easy) ** n_max) + (1 - (1 - p_hard) ** n_max)) / 2

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pass_at == sorted(set(pass_at)), "pass@N rises with N")
    check(abs(seq_per_success - 1 / p) < 1e-12, "Sequential retry costs 1/p per success")
    check(cost_ratio > 2, "Parallel pool costs over twice as much per success")
    check(abs(p_mix - p) < 1e-12, "Mixed workload has the same average rate")
    check(true_mix < naive_mix - 0.3, "Averaging p overstates mixed-workload pass@N")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, precision=0, style="prose")
    n_max_str = fmt_int(n_max)
    pools_str = MarkdownStr(", ".join(str(n) for n in pools[:-1]) + ", and " + str(pools[-1]))
    pass_1_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[0]))
    pass_2_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[1]))
    pass_4_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[2]))
    pass_max_str = fmt_percent(pass_max, precision=1, style="prose")
    last_gain_pts_str = fmt(last_gain * 100, precision=1)
    parallel_per_success_str = fmt(parallel_per_success, precision=1)
    seq_candidates_str = fmt(seq_candidates, precision=2)
    seq_per_success_str = fmt(seq_per_success, precision=1)
    cost_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cost_ratio, precision=1)
    p_easy_str = fmt_percent(p_easy, precision=0, style="prose")
    naive_mix_str = fmt_percent(naive_mix, precision=1, style="prose")
    true_mix_str = fmt_percent(true_mix, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price .callout-notebook title="The price of a larger pool"}

**Problem**: Each candidate repair passes the task's verifier with probability $p$, independently for this task, and the verifier is the acceptance check. How many candidates per accepted repair does a parallel pool of $N$ spend, compared with sequential retry that stops at the first pass and gives up after $N$ attempts?

**Variables**: $p$ = `{python} BestOfN.p_str` (hypothetical); pools of `{python} BestOfN.pools_str` candidates; a selector that returns a passing member whenever one exists.

**Math**: The formula pass@$N = 1-(1-p)^N$ gives `{python} BestOfN.pass_1_str`, `{python} BestOfN.pass_2_str`, `{python} BestOfN.pass_4_str`, and `{python} BestOfN.pass_max_str` for those pools. The last of `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates adds $p(1-p)^{N-1}$, only `{python} BestOfN.last_gain_pts_str` percentage points. The parallel pool always spends `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates, or `{python} BestOfN.parallel_per_success_str` per accepted repair. Sequential retry fails only when all `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` attempts fail, so it reaches the same `{python} BestOfN.pass_max_str`, yet it spends on average $[1-(1-p)^N]/p$ = `{python} BestOfN.seq_candidates_str` candidates, or $1/p$ = `{python} BestOfN.seq_per_success_str` per accepted repair.

**Systems insight**: At equal success, the parallel pool costs `{python} BestOfN.cost_mult_str` as much per accepted repair; what it buys is one round instead of an expected `{python} BestOfN.seq_candidates_str` sequential generate-and-check rounds. Breadth buys latency, not cost. In $C_{\text{eff}} = \mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]/p_{\text{acc}}$ it raises $p_{\text{acc}}$ per round but raises the attempt cost faster. Size $N$ as the smallest pool whose pass@$N$ meets the target within the rounds the deadline allows, and stop growing it once the next candidate's gain is worth less than its cost.

:::

### Paying for selection and evidence

Increasing breadth can make a useful candidate more likely to appear, but it also creates more material to inspect. Under a fixed budget, spending everything on generation may leave too little time to distinguish the candidates. A smaller pool with informative checks can outperform a larger pool with weak selection; the reverse is possible when generation coverage is the limiting factor. The comparison requires measuring the whole policy.

Checker errors need their own analysis. More candidates create more opportunities to encounter a false pass. The probability that the selected output is wrong, however, depends on the candidate distribution, the check's conditional error rates, and the rule for choosing among passing candidates, and search that adapts to a scoring rule changes all three.

The next design choice is where to obtain evidence. A final-result check may be sufficient for one task; another may benefit from checking an intermediate assumption before investing in its continuation. The next section examines outcome and process checks, including what their errors imply for an accepted candidate.

## Process Verification {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification}

The selector needs evidence that distinguishes a promising candidate from a merely plausible one. For the connection-pool repair, compiling a patch establishes that it satisfies the compiler's checks, while whether waiting workers are notified when a connection returns needs a different check. A targeted concurrent test supplies different evidence, but its schedules may still miss the suspected synchronization defect. Each check answers a bounded question. The allocation decision is which question to ask, when to ask it, and how its answer should change the remaining search.

### Outcome and step-level evidence

An **outcome check**\index{Outcome check!definition} assesses a completed candidate against a criterion, such as whether the repaired service passes a regression test. An **outcome reward model**\index{Outcome reward model!definition} instead predicts a score for the completed candidate. The distinction concerns where feedback is assigned, not necessarily what the evaluator sees: a learned outcome scorer can inspect the full reasoning trajectory as well as the final answer.

Step-level checks assess intermediate claims or transitions. In the repair task, a check might test whether a waiting worker receives the return notification before the agent implements a proposed timeout increase. If a controlled observation contradicts the timeout explanation, the runtime can redirect generation before spending the rest of the budget on its implementation. A learned process scorer can similarly rank or prune partial reasoning, and a low score is fallible evidence that a branch will fail. **Process supervision**\index{Process supervision!definition}[^fn-prm-step-labels] assigns feedback to intermediate reasoning steps rather than to final outcomes [@lightman2023let].

[^fn-prm-step-labels]: **Step-Level Labels (PRM800K)**: Outcome labels for code can be produced automatically by running tests. Step labels require a judgment on each intermediate step, and the PRM800K dataset used to train the process reward model of @lightman2023let contains about 800,000 human step-level labels. That labeling cost is one reason learned process scorers are scarcer than outcome checks. \index{Process reward model!labeling cost}

::: {#dfn-process-reward-model .callout-definition title="Process reward model (PRM)"}

***Process reward model***\index{Process reward model!definition} is a learned scorer that assigns a value to each intermediate step of a candidate trajectory, conditioned on the task and the preceding steps.

1.  **Significance**: Step scores let search prune a branch before it spends a full candidate's generation budget, which is what keeps beam and tree search within a finite budget (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth).
2.  **Distinction**: An outcome reward model scores only the completed candidate; a process reward model assigns credit at every step, so it can redirect generation earlier but needs step-level labels that cost far more to collect than test outcomes.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating a favorable step score as evidence of task success; a process reward model ranks and prunes, and occupies no closure evidence level.

:::

Each granularity catches failures the other misses. An outcome check can detect interactions that look harmless step by step. A process check can locate an error earlier, but checking too frequently consumes resources and can discard useful branches. The relevant benefit is avoided downstream work or better selection, weighed against checking cost and mistaken rejections.

The input scope matters as much as the number of checks. Consider a scorer that reads the task input of $P$ tokens and the candidate's prefix after each of its $J$ steps, each step adding $\ell$ tokens. Rescoring each growing prefix from scratch, without reusing the computation from the previous step, costs

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\left(P + j\,\ell\right) = J P + \frac{J(J+1)}{2}\,\ell
$$ {#eq-vol3-prm-rescoring}

scorer input tokens, which grows quadratically in the number of steps. The beam-search notebook later in this chapter (\ref{nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs}) bills exactly the sum in @eq-vol3-prm-rescoring, with $P$ excluded, for every retained prefix. Incremental evaluation removes the quadratic term when the evaluator and serving interface support prefix reuse; a scorer that requires the complete candidate pays it in full. Check scheduling therefore needs an explicit account of inputs, calls, and latency.

@Tbl-vol3-verifier-classes compares four common kinds of check by what they examine and what their verdicts can support. The last column places each on the closure evidence levels of @sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure. A learned scorer, however accurate on its evaluation set, occupies no closure evidence level. It ranks candidates and certifies none.

| **Check**                | **Evaluates**                      | **Coverage**                              | **False-acceptance exposure**                    | **Deterministic**           | **Closure evidence level**                             |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| Outcome scorer (learned) | Completed candidate                | Any representation it was trained to read | Persuasive but wrong final text                  | No                          | None; ranks only                                       |
| Process scorer (learned) | Intermediate step given its prefix | Steps it can delimit and judge            | Locally plausible steps that drift from the task | No                          | None; ranks and prunes only                            |
| Compiler or type checker | Syntax and declared types          | Properties expressible in the type system | Behavior outside the type system                 | Yes                         | Static check                                           |
| Sealed test suite        | Behavior on withheld cases         | The cases and schedules it exercises      | Untested inputs and schedules                    | Yes, under fixed conditions | Sealed test, if the candidate cannot read or modify it |

: **Kinds of check and the claims they support**: Learned scorers order candidates; compilers and sealed suites establish bounded properties. None dominates the others on every task, and a deterministic verdict remains incomplete outside its coverage. {#tbl-vol3-verifier-classes tbl-colwidths="[17,17,18,20,11,17]"}

The right check for a task is the one that can observe the failure the task cannot tolerate.

### Precision depends on the candidate pool

The preceding chapter separated structural validity from task acceptance. Search adds another question: among the candidates that pass a particular check, how many actually satisfy the task? Define the event $\mathrm{Valid}$ as satisfying the stipulated task specification and $\mathrm{PASS}$ as receiving the check's positive result. Let $p=P(\mathrm{Valid})$ be the valid-candidate rate in the pool being evaluated, $\epsilon_{\text{FA}}=P(\mathrm{PASS}\mid\neg\mathrm{Valid})$ the **false acceptance rate**\index{False acceptance rate!definition}, and $\epsilon_{\text{FR}}=P(\neg\mathrm{PASS}\mid\mathrm{Valid})$ the **false rejection rate**\index{False rejection rate!definition}. Here “acceptance” names a checker error category, not permission to deploy a patch.

The probability of a positive result is $q=p(1-\epsilon_{\text{FR}})+(1-p)\,\epsilon_{\text{FA}}$. Bayes' rule gives the precision of those positive results:

$$
\Pi_V \equiv P(\mathrm{Valid}\mid\mathrm{PASS})
=\frac{p(1-\epsilon_{\text{FR}})}{p(1-\epsilon_{\text{FR}})+(1-p)\,\epsilon_{\text{FA}}}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-verifier-precision}

A small false acceptance rate can still leave substantial error among passing candidates when most proposals are invalid, the base-rate effect familiar from diagnostic testing. The rates must be measured for the relevant task class, generator, and checking conditions.

@Eq-vol3-verifier-precision describes the passing population. Turning it into a claim about the *selected* candidate requires a selection policy. Consider independent, identically distributed candidate-and-check outcomes for a fixed task, with fixed conditional check-error rates. Generate a fixed batch, order it independently of candidate quality and check results, and select the first passing candidate in that order. Abstain if none passes. Conditional on a selection, its precision is $\Pi_V$. Reaching a later position means only that earlier candidates failed, and under these independence assumptions that history does not change the selected candidate's validity given that it passed. Choosing the highest continuous score instead selects on the scorer's errors as well as on quality, which @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure analyzes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: compute-vol3-ttc-check-yield
# ┌── LEGO ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under
# │ Goal: Separate passing-set precision, selection coverage, and incident loss.
# │ Show: A hypothetical fixed-batch first-pass selection policy.
# │ How: IID candidate/check outcomes, fixed rates, abstention if none passes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
import math

class CheckYield:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    n = 64
    tokens_per_candidate = 1_024 * token
    output_price = 15 * USD / Mtoken
    p = 0.05
    eps_fr = 0.10  # false rejection rate, epsilon_FR (hypothetical)
    eps_fa = 0.02  # false acceptance rate, epsilon_FA (hypothetical)
    incident_loss = 500 * USD

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Physics & Logic) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    valid_pass = p * (1 - eps_fr)
    invalid_pass = (1 - p) * eps_fa
    pass_probability = valid_pass + invalid_pass
    assert pass_probability > 0, "Passing-set precision requires q > 0."
    precision = valid_pass / pass_probability
    defect_given_selection = 1 - precision
    any_selection = 1 - (1 - pass_probability) ** n
    no_selection = 1 - any_selection
    wrong_selection = any_selection * defect_given_selection
    any_false_pass = 1 - (1 - invalid_pass) ** n
    expected_valid_passes = n * valid_pass
    expected_invalid_passes = n * invalid_pass
    expected_passes = n * pass_probability
    conditional_loss = defect_given_selection * incident_loss
    task_loss = wrong_selection * incident_loss
    output_bill = (n * tokens_per_candidate * output_price).to(USD)
    # Sensitivity: halve the false acceptance rate, or double the valid rate.
    precision_half_fa = valid_pass / (valid_pass + (1 - p) * eps_fa / 2)
    precision_double_p = 2 * p * (1 - eps_fr) / (2 * p * (1 - eps_fr) + (1 - 2 * p) * eps_fa)
    loss_to_bill = (task_loss / output_bill).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    assert isinstance(n, int) and n > 0
    assert all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (p, eps_fa, eps_fr))
    assert all(
        0 <= probability <= 1
        for probability in (
            valid_pass,
            invalid_pass,
            pass_probability,
            precision,
            defect_given_selection,
            any_selection,
            no_selection,
            wrong_selection,
            any_false_pass,
        )
    )
    assert math.isclose(precision + defect_given_selection, 1)
    assert math.isclose(any_selection + no_selection, 1)
    assert 0 <= expected_valid_passes <= n
    assert 0 <= expected_invalid_passes <= n
    assert 0 <= expected_passes <= n
    assert math.isclose(expected_valid_passes + expected_invalid_passes, expected_passes)
    assert wrong_selection <= any_selection
    assert wrong_selection <= any_false_pass
    assert math.isclose(wrong_selection, any_selection * defect_given_selection)
    assert tokens_per_candidate > 0 * token
    assert output_price >= 0 * USD / Mtoken
    assert output_bill >= 0 * USD
    assert 0 * USD <= task_loss <= conditional_loss <= incident_loss
    assert math.isclose(task_loss.to(USD).magnitude, (any_selection * conditional_loss).to(USD).magnitude)
    assert precision < precision_half_fa < 1 and precision < precision_double_p < 1
    assert loss_to_bill > 100

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Human-Readable Outputs) ───────────────────────────────────
    n_str = fmt_int(n)
    tokens_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_candidate)
    price_str = fmt_usd(output_price * Mtoken)
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, style="prose")
    eps_fr_str = fmt_percent(eps_fr, style="prose")
    eps_fa_str = fmt_percent(eps_fa, style="prose")
    loss_str = fmt_usd(incident_loss)
    valid_passes_str = fmt(expected_valid_passes, precision=2)
    invalid_passes_str = fmt(expected_invalid_passes, precision=3)
    passes_str = fmt(expected_passes, precision=3)
    precision_str = fmt_percent(precision, precision=2, style="prose")
    defect_str = fmt_percent(defect_given_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    coverage_str = fmt_percent(any_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    abstention_str = fmt_percent(no_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    wrong_str = fmt_percent(wrong_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    any_false_str = fmt_percent(any_false_pass, precision=2, style="prose")
    conditional_loss_str = fmt_usd(conditional_loss, precision=2)
    task_loss_str = fmt_usd(task_loss, precision=2)
    bill_str = fmt_usd(output_bill, precision=2)
    precision_half_fa_str = fmt_percent(precision_half_fa, precision=1, style="prose")
    precision_double_p_str = fmt_percent(precision_double_p, precision=1, style="prose")
    loss_to_bill_str = fmt_int(round(loss_to_bill))
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under .callout-notebook title="Yield and risk under asymmetric verifier error"}

**Problem**: A repair policy generates all `{python} CheckYield.n_str` candidates before selection. It uses the first-passing rule above and abstains when no candidate passes. What does additional breadth buy, and what risk remains?

**Variables**: All rates are hypothetical. Each candidate contains `{python} CheckYield.tokens_str` tokens, billed at `{python} CheckYield.price_str` per million output tokens. The valid-candidate rate is `{python} CheckYield.p_str`, false rejection is `{python} CheckYield.eps_fr_str`, and false acceptance is `{python} CheckYield.eps_fa_str`. Suppose a separately authorized deployment policy deploys the selected candidate without further checking. A defective deployment incurs `{python} CheckYield.loss_str` in incident loss. For this calculation alone, valid deployments and abstentions incur zero incident loss, and missed repairs and delay are left unpriced.

**Math**: The expected passing counts are `{python} CheckYield.valid_passes_str` valid candidates and `{python} CheckYield.invalid_passes_str` invalid candidates, totaling `{python} CheckYield.passes_str`. @Eq-vol3-verifier-precision yields `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` precision. Conditional on making a selection, the probability of a defective selection is therefore `{python} CheckYield.defect_str`, with expected incident loss `{python} CheckYield.conditional_loss_str` per selected deployment.

The probability of any selection is $1-(1-q)^N$, or `{python} CheckYield.coverage_str`; the policy abstains on `{python} CheckYield.abstention_str` of batches. Multiplying selection coverage by conditional defect probability gives `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str` defective selections per task attempt and `{python} CheckYield.task_loss_str` expected incident loss per attempt, including abstentions. Generating the entire batch costs `{python} CheckYield.bill_str` in output charges. Input charges, checking, and other operational costs are omitted. A sequential policy that stops generation at the first pass would have a different generation bill.

**Systems insight**: Expected incident loss per attempt is about `{python} CheckYield.loss_to_bill_str` times the output bill, so the acceptance policy, not the token price, sets the cost of this task. Precision responds to two knobs of similar strength: halving the false acceptance rate raises it from `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` to `{python} CheckYield.precision_half_fa_str`, and doubling the valid-candidate rate raises it to `{python} CheckYield.precision_double_p_str`. More candidates move neither. At a low base rate, spend on whichever of a better generator or a stricter check is cheaper, and price false rejections too when a missed valid repair is costly.

:::

At fixed $p$, $\epsilon_{\text{FA}}$, and $\epsilon_{\text{FR}}$, increasing $N$ does *not* change $\Pi_V$. It increases the chance of obtaining a passing candidate. It also increases the chance that the batch contains at least one false pass, $1-[1-(1-p)\,\epsilon_{\text{FA}}]^N$. In the example, that latter probability is `{python} CheckYield.any_false_str`, not the `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str` probability of actually selecting a defective candidate. A batch can contain a false pass while an earlier valid pass is selected. Candidate availability, checker precision, and selected-output risk are different quantities.

### When search changes the checking problem {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure}

The fixed-distribution calculation is the baseline, and adaptive search moves away from it. A policy that repeatedly revises candidates to improve a score changes the candidate distribution. Selecting extreme scores can also concentrate on regions where the evaluator is poorly calibrated. The original estimates of $p$, $\epsilon_{\text{FA}}$, and $\epsilon_{\text{FR}}$ may no longer describe the candidates being selected. Optimization against imperfect measures can fail through distinct mechanisms, including noisy measurements and changes in the relationship between a proxy and the desired outcome [@manheim2018categorizing]. Manheim and Garrabrant classify these as forms of Goodhart's law, the observation that a measure used as a target stops tracking what it measured, and three of their forms matter here. *Regressional* Goodhart arises because a noisy score partly measures its own error. *Extremal* Goodhart arises because a relationship between score and quality measured on ordinary candidates need not hold at the extremes that search reaches. *Adversarial* Goodhart arises when a candidate can influence the measurement itself.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-argmax-selection
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTION ON A NOISY SCORE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure.
# │ Goal: Show how argmax selection concentrates positive scoring error, and
# │       how a rare checker gap becomes likely in a large pool.
# │ Show: Exact expected maximum of N standard normal errors; exploit presence.
# │ How: Numerical integration of N x phi(x) Phi(x)^(N-1); IID candidates.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
import math

def expected_max_std_normal(n, lo=-10.0, hi=10.0, steps=40_000):
    """Trapezoidal integral of x * n * phi(x) * Phi(x)**(n - 1)."""
    dx = (hi - lo) / steps
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(steps + 1):
        x = lo + i * dx
        pdf = math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
        cdf = 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2)))
        weight = 0.5 if i in (0, steps) else 1.0
        total += weight * x * n * pdf * cdf ** (n - 1)
    return total * dx

class ArgmaxSelection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_small = 4  # hypothetical small pool
    n_large = 64  # same batch size as the yield notebook
    gap_rate = 0.005  # hypothetical fraction of candidates exploiting a check gap

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    shift_small = expected_max_std_normal(n_small)
    shift_large = expected_max_std_normal(n_large)
    asym_large = math.sqrt(2 * math.log(n_large))
    gap_present = 1 - (1 - gap_rate) ** n_large

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(expected_max_std_normal(1)) < 1e-6, "Mean of one standard normal is zero")
    check(0 < shift_small < shift_large < asym_large, "Selected error grows with N, below the asymptote")
    check(0 < gap_present < 1, "Probability bounds")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    n_small_str = fmt_int(n_small)
    n_large_str = fmt_int(n_large)
    shift_small_str = fmt(shift_small, precision=1)
    shift_large_str = fmt(shift_large, precision=1)
    asym_large_str = fmt(asym_large, precision=1)
    gap_rate_str = fmt_percent(gap_rate, precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_present_str = fmt_percent(gap_present, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The regressional mechanism can be stated exactly. Suppose a learned scorer reports $\hat U_i = U_i + \epsilon_i$ for candidate $i$, where $U_i$ is the quality the task cares about and $\epsilon_i$ is scoring error, independent across candidates with standard deviation $\sigma$. Selecting $\arg\max_i \hat U_i$ selects on the sum, so the winner is disproportionately a candidate whose error happened to be positive. For Gaussian errors, the expected largest error among $N$ candidates grows without bound, approaching

$$
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\max_{i \le N} \epsilon_i\Bigr] \approx \sigma\sqrt{2\ln N}
$$ {#eq-vol3-argmax-noise}

for large $N$. In units of $\sigma$, the exact expectation is about `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_small_str` for `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_small_str` candidates and `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_large_str` for `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str`, where the asymptotic form gives `{python} ArgmaxSelection.asym_large_str`. The winner's score therefore overstates its quality by an amount that grows with the pool. A score threshold calibrated on single ordinary candidates admits more errors when applied to the maximum of many, because the maximum is where the scorer's positive errors concentrate.

Measured best-of-$N$ selection against learned reward models shows the pattern: the optimized proxy score keeps rising with $N$, while a held-out reference score rises and then declines [@gao2023scaling]. @Eq-vol3-argmax-noise describes the drift that produces that divergence; it does not predict where the decline begins, which depends on how quality and error are distributed for the task. @Fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence sketches that divergence without values.

::: {#fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection**: A qualitative sketch of the measured best-of-$N$ pattern. The proxy score of the selected candidate keeps rising as $N$ grows, while a held-out reference score rises and then declines. The widening gap is the scoring error that argmax selection concentrates in the winner. The axes carry no values, and the point where the reference score turns down depends on the task." fig-alt="Line sketch with candidates selected from, N, on a log-scale horizontal axis and score of the selected candidate on the vertical axis, without tick values. A dashed blue curve labeled proxy score being maximized rises and flattens. A solid green curve labeled held-out reference score follows it at first, peaks near the middle, and then declines. The region between the curves is shaded, a red double-headed arrow at the right labels the gap scoring error of the winner, and a dashed line at the green peak notes that where the decline begins depends on the task."}
![](images/svg/goodhart_divergence.svg)
:::

Rare gaps in a check follow the same compounding as pass@$k$. If a fraction $\eta$ of candidates exploit something the check does not examine, a pool of $N$ contains at least one such candidate with probability $1-(1-\eta)^N$. A gap present in `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_rate_str` of candidates, too rare to notice when testing one candidate at a time, appears in a pool of `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` with probability `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_present_str`. If the exploit also scores well, selection finds it. The design rule follows: a check's accuracy on ordinary candidates overstates its accuracy on the candidates that search selects, and the gap widens with pool size.

For the connection-pool task, suppose the notification path is defective. A test-pass score can increase because a patch repairs that path, or because it removes the assertion that detects a worker remaining blocked after a connection returns. Both changes improve the measured score; only the first addresses the hypothesized defect. The candidate under evaluation must therefore be separated from the criteria that evaluate it, so that it can neither redefine the authoritative test nor manufacture its reported result. A candidate that executes in the same process as the test can go further and replace the assertion routine itself at run time, which is adversarial Goodhart in its most direct form; @sec-vol3-rlvr-rewards examines such exploits where training amplifies them. Isolation and enforcement belong to @sec-vol3-sandboxes; here the allocation consequence is that checking work pays only while its evidence stays trustworthy.

Protecting the evaluator leaves its coverage unchanged: a sealed test suite can miss an untested schedule, and a learned scorer can favor a persuasive but invalid explanation. Evaluation therefore examines the outputs selected by the actual search policy at the proposed budgets, including false acceptances and abstentions. More independent evidence can justify acceptance; another correlated score adds little.

Useful checking also produces information that later reasoning can reuse: which hypothesis was contradicted, which candidate version passed a test, and under which assumptions. A revised patch may invalidate an earlier result even if much of its text is unchanged. The next section makes those dependencies explicit so that a search policy can revise a candidate without treating every previous observation as either permanently valid or entirely disposable.

## Revisable Candidate Plans {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision}
