A check can challenge more than the final answer. Suppose the repair agent has proposed a diagnosis, a patch, and a plan for checking the connection-pool change. A targeted test then contradicts the diagnosis. Regenerating every part of the proposal would repeat work, but preserving every part would retain conclusions built on a rejected premise. The runtime needs to identify which candidate artifacts depend on that premise before choosing the scope of another model call.

A **revisable candidate plan**\index{Revisable candidate plan!definition} makes those dependencies explicit. It records proposed work and the evidence supporting it, not operations already performed, so the runtime can regenerate only the parts whose support has changed instead of the entire candidate. The revised parts still face the same checks.

### Making candidate dependencies explicit {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-plan-graph}

Consider the earlier candidate that attributes the connection-pool failure to an overly short timeout. The runtime can organize its supporting artifacts as a directed acyclic graph, with an edge from each prerequisite to the artifact that uses it. @Tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies gives a small example. The source excerpt and failure observation are recorded inputs; the diagnosis, proposed patch, and check selection are generated artifacts. The graph records dependencies between them without requiring the model's internal reasoning to have the same structure.

| Artifact                | Direct prerequisites                        | What the artifact contributes                                     |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source excerpt          | Repository revision and file identity       | The implementation being considered                               |
| Diagnosis               | Source excerpt and failure observation      | A proposed explanation of the failure                             |
| Patch candidate         | Source excerpt and diagnosis                | A proposed change to that implementation                          |
| Check selection         | Patch candidate and test inventory          | Checks intended to distinguish this repair from an inadequate one |
| API compatibility notes | Task constraints and public API declaration | Restrictions that every acceptable repair must preserve           |
: **Dependencies within a repair candidate**: Each row names the inputs needed to interpret its artifact. A separate compatibility branch can be retained only while its own inputs remain applicable. {#tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies}

The controlled waiter-and-return test shows a connection becoming available while the waiter remains blocked past the notification point. That observation undermines the timeout diagnosis as an adequate explanation of the observed failure and directs attention toward a missed return notification. The timeout-increasing patch and its check selection depend on the old diagnosis, so they require reconsideration as well. The source excerpt keeps its support while the file is unchanged, and the API compatibility notes keep theirs while the task constraints and API declaration are unchanged. The next request therefore asks for a revised diagnosis, patch, and check selection while supplying the still-applicable inputs, and the new diagnosis faces its own checks.

The runtime has to record and check these dependencies, because a graph with missing edges preserves unsupported conclusions as readily as an unstructured outline. An apparently separate compatibility branch may depend on the same source declaration as the patch; if that declaration changes, both branches become stale. The representation pays when its maintenance cost is lower than the repeated generation and checking it avoids.

### Tying evidence to its conditions {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-precondition-invalidation}

The runtime must distinguish a rejected claim from an observation that no longer applies. A failed targeted test can contradict the claim that a particular patch fixes the tested behavior. An earlier passing result for a different patch remains a true record of that patch and says nothing about the current one. Keeping the two apart prevents a stored success from becoming evidence for a candidate that was never checked.

For the repair task, a test observation should identify the source or patch version, test version, relevant build or environment configuration, and check that produced it. A file-read observation similarly refers to the file contents actually read, not to whatever later occupies the same path.

When a relevant input changes, the runtime marks affected artifacts as unsupported for the current candidate and follows the recorded dependencies to identify further artifacts needing review. If artifact $v$ loses support, the set needing review is its descendants, $\text{Desc}(v) = \{u \mid v \rightsquigarrow u\}$, where $v \rightsquigarrow u$ means a directed path leads from $v$ to $u$. A breadth-first traversal computes this set in time linear in the number of artifacts and dependency edges. Artifacts outside the set keep their support, which is what lets an independent branch such as the compatibility notes survive. For graphs of the size in @tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies, the traversal costs far less than generating a single token, so the price of dependency tracking lies in recording the edges correctly. @Fig-vol3-plan-revision traces this computation for the repair candidate and the scoped regeneration that follows it.

::: {#fig-vol3-plan-revision fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration**: In (A), the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis. Following the recorded dependency edges marks the patch and check selection for review, while the recorded inputs and the separately derived API notes keep their support. In (B), a new request supplies that supported frontier and regenerates only the diagnosis, patch, and check selection. The graph records candidate artifacts, not executed operations, and each replacement must still pass its own checks. The test inventory that also feeds check selection is omitted." fig-alt="Two stacked panels with the same dependency graph. Inputs on the left are source excerpt, failure observation, waiter-return test, and API declaration. In panel A, source excerpt and failure observation feed a diagnosis marked timeout too short, which feeds a patch candidate and then a check selection, both drawn with dashed red borders and labeled needs review. The waiter-return test points to the diagnosis with a dashed red arrow labeled contradicts. The API declaration feeds API notes labeled support kept. A text line reads Desc of diagnosis equals patch and check selection. In panel B, a dashed region labeled regenerated contains diagnosis prime labeled missed notification, patch candidate prime labeled notify on return, and check selection prime labeled ordering test, while the inputs and API notes are labeled retained."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-plan-revision.svg)
:::

Version identities make this decision reproducible, and the observation's assumptions complete it. A test that depends on a changing external service may cease to support the current task even when its local files have identical versions. Conversely, an unrelated file edit need not invalidate a result whose relevant inputs and execution conditions are unchanged. Reuse rests on the assumptions of the observation, including what the check covered and what it omitted, rather than on age or filename alone.

The graph represents candidate artifacts and their support; reading files, applying patches, and running tests, even in a sandbox, are real operations governed by the runtime's permissions and resource limits. Deleting a candidate node leaves a file edit, an external resource, or any other effect in place, so execution and recovery mechanisms account for those effects separately (@sec-vol3-failure-recovery).

### Choosing the revision scope {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics}

A local revision request supplies the current task constraints, the retained inputs relevant to the change, the observation that challenges the candidate, and the artifacts to replace. In the example, it asks for a new explanation and corresponding patch and check selection, not a fresh statement of unchanged API requirements. The runtime then checks that the replacements agree with the retained artifacts and that their dependency claims are adequate. A locally coherent replacement can still conflict with the rest of the candidate.

Revision scope falls into three tiers, ordered by how much support the new evidence removes. A **local repair**\index{Local repair!definition} replaces one artifact while preserving what its dependents rely on, such as a corrected command that yields the same output, so the dependency graph is unchanged. A **subgraph resynthesis**\index{Subgraph resynthesis!definition} replaces the artifact and its descendants. The request supplies the still-supported frontier and asks the model to bridge from it to the downstream requirements that remain unchanged; the repair example, which replaces the diagnosis, patch, and check selection while keeping the source excerpt and compatibility notes, is this tier. When an observation falsifies a premise of the task itself, such as a missing capability or a revoked permission, no revision of the candidate can restore support. Deliberation then stops and the task is reported as unresolved or escalated under its contract rather than given more generation. @Fig-vol3-hierarchical-revision arranges the three tiers as two questions the runtime asks about the new evidence.

::: {#fig-vol3-hierarchical-revision fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Choosing the Revision Scope**: Two questions about the new evidence select among three responses. If the artifact's dependents still have what they need, a local repair replaces it alone. If they do not but the task's premises hold, subgraph resynthesis replaces the artifact and its descendants. If a premise has failed, deliberation stops and the task is reported unresolved or escalated. The tiers order responses by how much support the evidence removes; they do not make the smallest edit the preferred one." fig-alt="Flowchart. A box reading new evidence removes support from an artifact leads to a diamond asking whether dependents' needs are still met. Yes leads down to a card labeled local repair: replace one artifact, dependency graph unchanged, for example a corrected command with the same output. No leads right to a second diamond asking whether task premises still hold. Yes leads to a card labeled subgraph resynthesis: replace the artifact and its descendants, bridge from the supported frontier, the connection-pool repair. No leads to a red card labeled stop deliberation: no revision restores support, report unresolved or escalate under the contract. An arrow along the bottom runs from less support removed to more support removed."}
![](images/svg/hierarchical_revision_mechanics.svg)
:::

Local revision is the cheapest option, not always the best. If the diagnosis changes the meaning of the task, the dependency record is unreliable, or most of the candidate shares the rejected assumption, full regeneration may be easier to evaluate. It also has a cost: unchanged material must be produced again, and the new candidate can introduce differences beyond the original defect. The decision compares the scope of lost support with the generation and checking work needed to restore it.

```{python}
#| label: lego-candidate-plan-revision
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CANDIDATE PLAN REVISION OUTPUT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics,
# │          nbk-03-compute-and-token-savings-of.
# │ Goal: Compare output tokens for full and scoped candidate regeneration.
# │ Show: Generated token counts, retained output share, and avoided output.
# │ How: Hypothetical equal-sized nodes; only replaced nodes are generated.
# │ Note: Excludes input processing, checks, scheduling, and physical effects.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class PlanRevision:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    total_nodes = 12  # hypothetical complete candidate size
    replacement_nodes = 3  # hypothetical affected subset
    tokens_per_node = 150 * count  # hypothetical generated tokens per node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    full_output = total_nodes * tokens_per_node
    local_output = replacement_nodes * tokens_per_node
    output_share = (local_output / full_output).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    avoided_share = 1 - output_share

    # ┌── 3. AUDIT (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    assert 0 < replacement_nodes <= total_nodes
    assert local_output <= full_output
    assert 0 <= avoided_share < 1

    # ┌── 4. EXPORT (Narrative Values) ─────────────────────────────────────
    total_nodes_str = fmt_count(total_nodes)
    replacement_nodes_str = fmt_count(replacement_nodes)
    tokens_per_node_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_node)
    full_output_str = fmt_tokens(full_output)
    local_output_str = fmt_tokens(local_output)
    output_share_str = fmt_percent(output_share, style="prose")
    avoided_share_str = fmt_percent(avoided_share, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-and-token-savings-of .callout-notebook title="Output cost of a local plan revision"}

**Problem**: Suppose a candidate contains `{python} PlanRevision.total_nodes_str` nodes, each requiring `{python} PlanRevision.tokens_per_node_str` generated tokens. New evidence leaves `{python} PlanRevision.replacement_nodes_str` nodes needing replacement. How much output does scoped regeneration avoid if either approach produces a candidate adequate for the same subsequent checks?

**Math**: Multiplying the complete node count by the output per node gives `{python} PlanRevision.full_output_str` tokens for full regeneration. Multiplying the replacement count by the same output allowance gives `{python} PlanRevision.local_output_str` tokens for scoped regeneration. The scoped request generates `{python} PlanRevision.output_share_str` of the full request's output, avoiding `{python} PlanRevision.avoided_share_str` of that output under the equal-node-size assumption.

**Systems insight**: Scoped regeneration saves exactly the fraction of the plan that keeps its support. The saving shrinks linearly as the contradicted premise reaches more descendants and vanishes when every node depends on it, so once most of the plan shares the rejected assumption, full regeneration costs little more and is easier to check. The count covers generated plan tokens only; input to interpret retained constraints, integration, and checking are charged to both options.

:::

The example isolates the benefit of changing less generated material. Whether that benefit survives in a complete system depends on the cost of maintaining dependencies, constructing the scoped input, and checking the replacement, all of which belong in the same evaluation as the avoided output. A candidate plan that must outlive one decision becomes live plan state, which @sec-vol3-agent-harness manages during execution and @sec-vol3-durable-execution preserves across failures.

### Bounding repeated revision {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-replanning-thrashing}

A candidate can be revised repeatedly without becoming better supported. The model may alternate between diagnoses, produce cosmetically different patches, or respond to an irrelevant warning by regenerating useful material. The runtime should ask what changed in the evidence or assumptions and which claim the revision is intended to resolve. A warning matters when it affects that claim; its severity label alone does not decide whether the candidate remains valid.

Revision therefore needs a remaining allowance for calls, tokens, checks, and elapsed time. Each admitted revision consumes that allowance, including unsuccessful local edits. Exhausting it stops further search or routes the unresolved task through an authorized handoff, and the current candidate stays unaccepted. Repeated equivalent proposals under unchanged conditions are a signal to stop early; a similar proposal under changed conditions is a new attempt.

Explicit dependencies let the runtime reuse support that remains applicable and focus generation where it does not. The next question is how to allocate a finite allowance across such revisions, competing candidates, and their checks. That requires an account of the work already spent and the work still admitted by the search policy.

## Search Stopping Criteria {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search}

The repair agent can generate another complete patch, extend a partial candidate by one step, or run a diagnostic that distinguishes competing explanations. Each choice consumes part of the same task budget, but it creates different dependencies. A check that guides the next extension lies on the critical path; independent candidates may proceed concurrently; an abandoned branch still incurs the work already performed. Choosing a search policy therefore requires an account of both the work admitted and the conditions under which further work should stop.

### Where search prunes candidates

Flat sampling generates a bounded set of complete candidates before selecting among them. In best-of-$N$, the runtime admits at most $N$ candidates and applies a selector to the completed, eligible outputs. The requests are independent, so available service capacity shortens elapsed time through concurrency, to the extent the service actually runs them together at an unchanged rate. Flat sampling also postpones semantic pruning until a complete candidate exists, which can spend tokens on a candidate that an earlier check would have rejected.

**Beam search**\index{Beam search!definition} makes that earlier decision explicit. The runtime retains partial candidates up to a fixed beam width, generates a bounded number of extensions of each retained candidate, scores the extensions, and retains the next beam. When a frontier contains fewer candidates than the beam width, it expands only those present; the root is not a full beam. Scores can combine learned estimates with checks available at that stage. The retained beam bounds which candidates receive further generation, not all live state: before pruning, the new extensions can number the beam width times the extensions per candidate, alongside their scores and retained ancestors.

Early pruning exchanges generation work for selection work and a stronger dependence on intermediate judgments. If the scorer discards a prefix that would have led to a good repair, this bounded run will not recover that prefix unless its policy explicitly permits revisiting it. Conversely, rejecting an invalid partial patch avoids completing and testing it. Pruning pays when these decisions cost less than the generation they avoid and discard few prefixes that would have succeeded.

An adaptive tree policy need not expand every retained candidate equally. Tree search over intermediate reasoning steps [@yao2023tree] can allocate another extension or rollout to a branch whose score is promising, whose outcome remains uncertain, or whose failure would clarify another decision. **Monte Carlo tree search**\index{Monte Carlo tree search!definition} is one way to maintain visit counts and estimated returns for this allocation. A widely used selection rule, introduced with the AlphaGo system [@silver2016mastering], descends from the root choosing at each partial candidate $s$ the extension $a$ that maximizes

$$
Q(s,a) + c_{\text{explore}}\,P(a \mid s)\,\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{a'} N(s,a')}}{1 + N(s,a)},
$$ {#eq-vol3-puct}

where $Q(s,a)$ is the mean value observed after that extension, $N(s,a)$ its visit count, $P(a \mid s)$ a prior over extensions, for a language model its probability of proposing that step, and $c_{\text{explore}}$ a constant that trades exploiting high values against exploring plausible, rarely visited extensions. After the runtime evaluates a new leaf and obtains value $V$, each edge on the path updates $N \leftarrow N + 1$ and $Q \leftarrow Q + (V - Q)/N$, a running mean. When $V$ comes from a learned scorer, the $Q$ term of @eq-vol3-puct inherits the selection drift of @eq-vol3-argmax-noise, and the rule steers visits toward edges whose estimates are high partly because they are noisy. The tree decides where to spend the next unit of work; noisy scores, changing observations, and a finite budget bound what it can establish, and it pays only when its allocation decisions justify their evaluation and state-management costs.

@Fig-vol3-search-topologies draws the three structures side by side, and @tbl-vol3-search-topologies summarizes where each structure prunes and what state it must hold. Sharing a common prefix among branches is a serving mechanism developed in @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree; the last column records only whether a structure's branches can use it.

::: {#fig-vol3-search-topologies fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where Each Search Structure Prunes**: Best-of-$N$ generates complete candidates independently and discards all but the selected one only at the end. Beam search generates the beam width times the extensions per candidate at each step, scores them, and keeps the beam width. Tree search expands the leaf its selection rule favors, evaluates it, and updates visit counts and value estimates along the path to the root. The drawings show structure only; the pool size, beam width, and depth are illustrative." fig-alt="Three panels of node diagrams. Best-of-N: a prompt node branches into four chains of three generated nodes each; past a dashed line labeled select, one final node is marked selected and three are marked pruned. Beam: a prompt node branches into two nodes, each of which generates two children; a dashed line labeled score, keep 2 marks two children pruned, the two survivors each generate two more, and a second dashed line labeled keep 2 marks two retained and two pruned. Tree search: an uneven tree in which one path from the prompt is drawn bold and ends at a new leaf labeled evaluated V, with a note that the bold path updates N and Q; other nodes are drawn dashed as not yet expanded. A legend identifies prompt, generated, retained or selected, generated then pruned, and not yet expanded nodes."}
![](images/svg/search_topologies_comparison.svg)
:::

| **Structure** | **Where pruning happens**                | **Concurrency**                               | **Search state**                                         | **Prefix sharing**                       |
|:--------------|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Best-of-$N$   | After complete candidates, at selection  | All $N$ requests independent                  | $N$ candidates and their check results                   | The common prompt only                   |
| Beam          | At each step boundary, by step score     | Within a step; stages wait for scoring        | Up to width times extensions before pruning, plus scores | Each retained prefix with its extensions |
| Tree search   | Adaptively, by value estimate and visits | Irregular; depends on which leaves are chosen | Tree nodes with visit counts and value estimates         | Every node's ancestors along its path    |

: **Search structures compared**: Each structure moves the pruning decision to a different point and holds different state. Concurrency describes the dependency graph; actual overlap depends on service capacity. {#tbl-vol3-search-topologies tbl-colwidths="[13,22,21,23,21]"}

### How pruning bounds tree growth {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-pruned-tree
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRUNED TREE GROWTH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth.
# │ Goal: Show how a step check's rejection rate bounds expected tree size.
# │ Show: Unpruned leaf explosion; effective branching factor; generated nodes.
# │ How: Independent rejection of each child; generated nodes are b times the
# │      surviving parents at each depth; equal-sized steps.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class PrunedTree:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    wide_b = 4  # hypothetical alternatives per step, unpruned illustration
    wide_depth = 10  # hypothetical steps, unpruned illustration
    b = 5  # hypothetical children proposed per retained node
    p_prune = 0.68  # hypothetical probability a step check rejects a child
    depth = 3  # hypothetical steps in the worked example

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    wide_leaves = wide_b**wide_depth
    b_eff = b * (1 - p_prune)
    critical_prune = 1 - 1 / b
    unpruned_generated = 0
    pruned_generated = 0.0
    for d in range(1, depth + 1):
        unpruned_generated += b**d
        pruned_generated += b * b_eff ** (d - 1)
    unpruned_leaves = b**depth
    pruned_leaves = b_eff**depth
    generated_saving = 1 - pruned_generated / unpruned_generated

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(wide_leaves > 1_000_000, "Unpruned illustration exceeds a million leaves")
    check(b_eff > 1, "Worked example remains supercritical")
    check(p_prune < critical_prune, "Rejection rate is below the subcritical threshold")
    check(pruned_generated < unpruned_generated, "Pruning reduces generated nodes")
    check(generated_saving > p_prune, "Node saving exceeds the per-child rejection rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    wide_b_str = fmt_int(wide_b)
    wide_depth_str = fmt_int(wide_depth)
    wide_leaves_str = fmt_int(wide_leaves)
    b_str = fmt_int(b)
    p_prune_str = fmt_percent(p_prune, precision=0, style="prose")
    depth_str = fmt_int(depth)
    b_eff_str = fmt(b_eff, precision=1)
    critical_prune_str = fmt_percent(critical_prune, precision=0, style="prose")
    unpruned_generated_str = fmt_int(unpruned_generated)
    pruned_generated_str = fmt(pruned_generated, precision=1)
    unpruned_leaves_str = fmt_int(unpruned_leaves)
    pruned_leaves_str = fmt(pruned_leaves, precision=1)
    generated_saving_str = fmt_percent(generated_saving, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Pruning is what keeps a search tree finite in practice. A tree that expands every node into `{python} PrunedTree.wide_b_str` children for `{python} PrunedTree.wide_depth_str` steps holds `{python} PrunedTree.wide_leaves_str` leaves, far beyond any per-task budget. Suppose instead that each node proposes $b$ children and a step check rejects each child independently with probability $p_{\text{prune}}$. The expected number of surviving children per node, the **effective branching factor**\index{Effective branching factor!definition}, is

$$
b_{\text{eff}} = b\,(1 - p_{\text{prune}}).
$$ {#eq-vol3-effective-branching}

Under @eq-vol3-effective-branching, the expected frontier at depth $d$ is $b_{\text{eff}}^{\,d}$, and every surviving node at depth $d-1$ generates and checks $b$ children, so the expected number of generated nodes through depth $D$ is $\sum_{d=1}^{D} b\,b_{\text{eff}}^{\,d-1}$. This is a Galton–Watson branching process. When $b_{\text{eff}} < 1$, which requires rejecting more than $1 - 1/b$ of proposals, the expected frontier shrinks with depth and the tree dies out on its own. When $b_{\text{eff}} > 1$, the frontier grows geometrically, and only the depth, token, and deadline ceilings stop it.

For a worked example with hypothetical rates, let each node propose `{python} PrunedTree.b_str` children, let the check reject `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` of them, and let the search run `{python} PrunedTree.depth_str` steps deep. The effective branching factor is then `{python} PrunedTree.b_eff_str`, still above one, because with `{python} PrunedTree.b_str` children per node the subcritical threshold is a rejection rate of `{python} PrunedTree.critical_prune_str`. The unpruned tree generates `{python} PrunedTree.unpruned_generated_str` nodes and ends with `{python} PrunedTree.unpruned_leaves_str` leaves. The pruned tree generates about `{python} PrunedTree.pruned_generated_str` nodes in expectation and keeps about `{python} PrunedTree.pruned_leaves_str` leaves, avoiding `{python} PrunedTree.generated_saving_str` of node generations. The saving exceeds the per-child rejection rate because each rejection also removes the subtree the child would have grown. With equal-sized steps, the avoided generation tokens follow the same ratio; each rejected child was still generated and scored before it was discarded.

Two cautions follow from the same model. A step check with false rejections removes valid subtrees along with invalid ones, so the saving is worth having only if its false rejection rate is acceptable. When the runtime needs just one accepted step, sequential generation needs $1/(1 - p_{\text{prune}})$ attempts in expectation, while generating $W$ candidates per round needs $1/(1 - p_{\text{prune}}^{\,W})$ rounds, each doing $W$ times the work. Batching buys fewer sequential rounds with more total generation, the same trade as breadth.

### Keeping branch evidence separate {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-mutable-sandbox-search}

A partial patch is a candidate artifact. Running its test is an actual operation on an environment. If one branch edits the shared working copy and a sibling then runs against those edits, the sibling's result no longer describes its own proposed repair. The runtime must associate each observation with the candidate and workspace version that produced it. Mutating alternatives need separate working environments or a controlled restoration procedure that establishes the intended baseline before the next branch executes.

Isolation has resource consequences even when the search ultimately discards every candidate. Branches consume workspace capacity, process slots, and tool time, and their retained observations occupy task state. A read-only probe also requires permission and can expose information. Pruning a candidate removes it from consideration; it does not reverse a sent message or prove that a remote operation stopped. The containment mechanisms in @sec-vol3-sandboxes enforce the environmental boundary. Search policy must budget the operations it requests without assuming that a tree edge makes an effect reversible.

### A resource ledger for the whole search

The runtime needs separate accounts for expenditure, work, elapsed time, and live state. Monetary expenditure can add generator, checker, and tool charges after expressing each in the same currency. Work counts remain distinct: generator input and output tokens, scorer input tokens, test invocations, and tool operations measure different demands. An estimate in FLOPs cannot be added to a test duration in seconds to obtain a meaningful total.

Elapsed time depends on the schedule connecting those demands. Sequential stages add along a path, concurrent jobs occupy overlapping intervals, and a bounded worker pool executes excess jobs in waves. Peak live state is a different quantity again. It includes the largest simultaneously retained set of candidate contexts, artifacts, and execution environments, not the cumulative number of candidates ever generated. A policy can reduce total output tokens while increasing input processing, scheduling barriers, or retained state. Keeping these accounts separate exposes the trade-off before a single cost metric hides it.

```{python}
#| label: lego-bounded-search-ledger
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BOUNDED SEARCH RESOURCE LEDGER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search,
# │          nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs.
# │ Goal: Compare counted work, token charges, and scheduled time for two
# │       hypothetical policies without assigning either a quality advantage.
# │ Show: Expansion counts, input/output/scorer tokens, prices, and time.
# │ How: Registry-derived output allowance; explicit local workload, prices,
# │      concurrency, and nonoverlapping generation/scoring/test stages.
# │ Note: No prefix-reuse discount. Prefill and service overheads are omitted
# │       from the timing subtotal, not from generator input-token charges.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
from math import ceil

class SearchLedger:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    steps = 4  # hypothetical candidate length in equal-sized segments
    step_tokens = 128  # hypothetical newly generated tokens per extension
    prompt_tokens = 4096  # hypothetical common task prompt per request
    flat_candidates = 16  # hypothetical complete-candidate budget
    beam_width = 4  # hypothetical retained-prefix limit
    extensions = 3  # hypothetical extensions per retained prefix
    generation_slots = 8  # hypothetical concurrent streams, unchanged rate
    test_slots = 8  # hypothetical concurrent isolated test runs
    score_time = 15 * ms  # fixed scenario allowance per FULL-prefix score
    test_time = 0.5 * second  # fixed scenario allowance per final test
    price_in = 3 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical generator input rate
    price_out = 15 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical output rate
    price_score = 0.50 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical scorer input rate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * weight_bytes
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    retained = 1
    frontier_counts = []
    beam_prompt_tokens = 0
    scorer_tokens = 0
    beam_waves = 0
    for depth in range(1, steps + 1):
        expanded = retained * extensions
        frontier_counts.append(expanded)
        beam_prompt_tokens += expanded * (prompt_tokens + (depth - 1) * step_tokens)
        # The scorer reads each complete generated prefix, not only its suffix.
        scorer_tokens += expanded * depth * step_tokens
        beam_waves += ceil(expanded / generation_slots)
        retained = min(beam_width, expanded)
    beam_segments = sum(frontier_counts)
    beam_output_tokens = beam_segments * step_tokens
    flat_length = steps * step_tokens
    flat_output_tokens = flat_candidates * flat_length
    flat_prompt_tokens = flat_candidates * prompt_tokens
    flat_waves = ceil(flat_candidates / generation_slots)
    flat_test_waves = ceil(flat_candidates / test_slots)
    beam_test_waves = ceil(retained / test_slots)
    flat_generation_time = flat_waves * flat_length * token_time
    beam_generation_time = beam_waves * step_tokens * token_time
    beam_scoring_time = beam_segments * score_time
    flat_elapsed = flat_generation_time + flat_test_waves * test_time
    beam_elapsed = beam_generation_time + beam_scoring_time + beam_test_waves * test_time
    flat_token_cost = flat_prompt_tokens * count * price_in + flat_output_tokens * count * price_out
    beam_token_cost = beam_prompt_tokens * count * price_in + beam_output_tokens * count * price_out + scorer_tokens * count * price_score
    output_saving = 1 - beam_output_tokens / flat_output_tokens
    # Break-even: the input-price fraction (e.g. under prefix caching) at which
    # the beam's output saving net of scoring pays for its repeated input.
    out_saving_usd = ((flat_output_tokens - beam_output_tokens) * count * price_out).to(USD)
    scorer_usd = (scorer_tokens * count * price_score).to(USD)
    input_premium_usd = ((beam_prompt_tokens - flat_prompt_tokens) * count * price_in).to(USD)
    breakeven_input_share = ((out_saving_usd - scorer_usd) / input_premium_usd).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(frontier_counts == [3, 9, 12, 12], "Root expansion precedes a full beam")
    check(beam_segments == 36 and retained == 4, "Count extensions before pruning")
    check(flat_output_tokens == 8192 and beam_output_tokens == 4608, "Count generated suffixes once")
    check(scorer_tokens == 13440, "Full-prefix scoring rereads ancestor tokens")
    check(beam_prompt_tokens == 156288 and flat_prompt_tokens == 65536, "Bill every supplied prompt without reuse discount")
    check(beam_waves == 7 and flat_waves == 2, "Apply generation concurrency to each stage")
    check(abs(output_saving - 0.4375) < 1e-12, "Beam generates fewer output tokens in this scenario")
    check(beam_token_cost > flat_token_cost, "Repeated inputs reverse the token-charge ranking")
    check(0 < breakeven_input_share < 1, "Beam breaks even only at a discounted input price")
    check(22 * second < flat_elapsed < 23 * second, "Flat timing subtotal remains in its stated range")
    check(19 * second < beam_elapsed < 21 * second, "Beam timing subtotal remains in its stated range")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    steps_str = fmt_count(steps)
    step_tokens_str = fmt_count(step_tokens)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(prompt_tokens)
    flat_candidates_str = fmt_count(flat_candidates)
    beam_width_str = fmt_count(beam_width)
    extensions_str = fmt_count(extensions)
    generation_slots_str = fmt_count(generation_slots)
    test_slots_str = fmt_count(test_slots)
    token_time_ms_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit=ms, precision=3)
    score_time_ms_str = fmt_time(score_time, unit=ms, precision=0)
    test_time_s_str = fmt_time(test_time, unit=second, precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * MILLION * count, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * MILLION * count, precision=0)
    price_score_str = fmt_usd(price_score * MILLION * count, precision=2)
    frontier_counts_str = MarkdownStr(", ".join(str(n) for n in frontier_counts))
    beam_segments_str = fmt_count(beam_segments)
    flat_length_str = fmt_count(flat_length)
    flat_output_tokens_str = fmt_count(flat_output_tokens)
    beam_output_tokens_str = fmt_count(beam_output_tokens)
    flat_prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(flat_prompt_tokens)
    beam_prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(beam_prompt_tokens)
    scorer_tokens_str = fmt_count(scorer_tokens)
    flat_waves_str = fmt_count(flat_waves)
    beam_waves_str = fmt_count(beam_waves)
    flat_test_waves_str = fmt_count(flat_test_waves)
    beam_test_waves_str = fmt_count(beam_test_waves)
    beam_scoring_time_s_str = fmt_time(beam_scoring_time, unit=second, precision=2)
    flat_elapsed_s_str = fmt_time(flat_elapsed, unit=second, precision=2)
    beam_elapsed_s_str = fmt_time(beam_elapsed, unit=second, precision=2)
    flat_token_cost_str = fmt_usd(flat_token_cost, precision=4)
    beam_token_cost_str = fmt_usd(beam_token_cost, precision=4)
    output_saving_pct_str = fmt_percent(output_saving, precision=2, style="prose")
    input_premium_usd_str = fmt_usd(input_premium_usd, precision=3)
    out_saving_usd_str = fmt_usd(out_saving_usd, precision=3)
    breakeven_input_share_str = fmt_percent(breakeven_input_share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs .callout-notebook title="Flat sampling vs. bounded beam expansion"}

**Problem**: A coding agent generates candidate patches in `{python} SearchLedger.steps_str` segments of `{python} SearchLedger.step_tokens_str` tokens. Compare `{python} SearchLedger.flat_candidates_str` complete candidates with beam width `{python} SearchLedger.beam_width_str` and `{python} SearchLedger.extensions_str` extensions per retained prefix. How do early pruning and repeated scoring change the resource ledger?

**Setup**: Every generator request supplies the same `{python} SearchLedger.prompt_tokens_str`-token task prompt plus its retained generated prefix. The illustrative output allowance from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost is `{python} SearchLedger.token_time_ms_str` per token. Assume `{python} SearchLedger.generation_slots_str` generation streams can maintain that allowance concurrently. The scorer reads the entire generated prefix, excluding the common task prompt, and processes requests serially at a fixed `{python} SearchLedger.score_time_ms_str` per request regardless of prefix length. Each final test takes `{python} SearchLedger.test_time_s_str`, with `{python} SearchLedger.test_slots_str` isolated runs available concurrently. Generation, scoring, and final testing do not overlap in this schedule.

Hypothetical prices per million tokens are `{python} SearchLedger.price_in_str` for generator input, `{python} SearchLedger.price_out_str` for output, and `{python} SearchLedger.price_score_str` for scorer input. Input charges include every supplied token, without a prefix-reuse discount. The timing subtotal omits prefill, queueing, request transfer, workspace preparation, and cleanup. It is not a prediction of complete service latency, and the token-charge subtotal excludes execution and infrastructure charges.

**Math**: Multiplying `{python} SearchLedger.flat_candidates_str` candidates by `{python} SearchLedger.flat_length_str` output tokens per candidate gives `{python} SearchLedger.flat_output_tokens_str` output tokens. Multiplying the same candidate count by the common prompt length gives `{python} SearchLedger.flat_prompt_tokens_str` input tokens. Generation occupies `{python} SearchLedger.flat_waves_str` waves of complete candidates, followed by `{python} SearchLedger.flat_test_waves_str` test waves. Multiplying the generation waves by candidate length and the per-token allowance, then adding the test waves times test duration, gives `{python} SearchLedger.flat_elapsed_s_str`. Multiplying each token count by its corresponding price gives a token-charge subtotal of `{python} SearchLedger.flat_token_cost_str`.

The beam expands frontiers of `{python} SearchLedger.frontier_counts_str` extensions in successive stages. Adding these counts gives `{python} SearchLedger.beam_segments_str` newly generated segments; multiplying by the segment length gives `{python} SearchLedger.beam_output_tokens_str` output tokens. After each stage it retains at most the beam width. For each request, generator input is the common prompt plus the preceding generated segments; summing across requests gives `{python} SearchLedger.beam_prompt_tokens_str` input tokens. The scorer instead reads each complete generated prefix, including its new segment. Summing each stage's extension count times its prefix length gives `{python} SearchLedger.scorer_tokens_str` scorer-input tokens. Generation requires `{python} SearchLedger.beam_waves_str` waves of one-segment requests; serial scoring adds `{python} SearchLedger.beam_scoring_time_s_str`; the final survivors fit in `{python} SearchLedger.beam_test_waves_str` test wave. Applying the same duration and price arithmetic gives `{python} SearchLedger.beam_elapsed_s_str` and `{python} SearchLedger.beam_token_cost_str`.

**Systems insight**: The beam generates `{python} SearchLedger.output_saving_pct_str` fewer output tokens, worth `{python} SearchLedger.out_saving_usd_str`, but resupplying the task prompt and retained prefixes to every extension costs `{python} SearchLedger.input_premium_usd_str` more in input, so its token bill is the higher one. The knob is the price of repeated input: the beam's bill falls below flat sampling's only when input tokens cost less than `{python} SearchLedger.breakeven_input_share_str` of list price, the regime a prefix cache creates (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree). Its shorter generation waves already give it the lower timing subtotal under this schedule, before omitted prefill is added back. Quality is not in this ledger; the choice between the two rests on the check results each produces.

:::

### Admission limits and pending work

A task-wide quota constrains new admissions before dispatch, because an overrun noticed after concurrent requests complete has already been spent. Before dispatching an extension, the runtime reserves its allowed output and any bounded check or tool work needed by the policy. Spent work plus outstanding reservations must remain within the relevant ceiling. Unused allowance becomes available again only when the runtime has sufficient evidence that the corresponding request can incur no further charge. An exact global spending limit therefore requires the service to provide an enforceable bound or trustworthy settlement information; local bookkeeping alone supplies an estimate.

The same policy must distinguish depth from time. A depth limit bounds sequential extensions or tool steps, while a deadline bounds how long the task owner will wait. At the deadline, the runtime stops admitting work, stops using late results for the expired decision, and requests cancellation where supported. A local cancellation is a request, not proof of remote termination, so pending operations remain in the ledger until their status is resolved; this is the same boundary established by the normalized status envelope (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract).

Resource exhaustion ends search without relaxing acceptance. A completed candidate may still fail the task's checks, and a high score is not permission to dispatch an action. If no retained result meets the acceptance criteria, the system reports an incomplete outcome, abstains, or escalates under the contract, even when every branch ran out of tokens. Mechanical limits bound expenditure independently of the model's request to continue, as required by the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

### Early exit and the value of continuation

Some tasks seek the first result that meets stated acceptance criteria, an objective called **satisficing**\index{Satisficing!definition}. Once a candidate satisfies the required evidence standard and any approval conditions, the policy stops searching for alternatives. A compiler pass supports only the property the compiler checked, and stopping generation leaves authorization, application, and acceptance in the target environment as separate steps.

An optimization objective can justify further work even after a candidate becomes acceptable. A task might prefer a smaller patch or lower runtime overhead within its remaining budget. Conversely, a candidate with a rising learned score may not justify further work if held-out evaluation shows that such score increases rarely improve accepted outcomes. The stopping rule must therefore state what benefit it values rather than assume that any passing check makes additional work worthless.

**Marginal stopping**\index{Marginal stopping!definition} compares the estimated benefit of the next admissible action with its additional cost. During an unresolved repair, the runtime does not know the true success probability it would obtain after another attempt. It needs estimates calibrated on held-out tasks with comparable conditions, or observable progress signals whose predictive value has been tested. A changed diagnostic or a newly passing regression check can inform such an estimate, but neither directly measures a probability of complete correctness. The estimate remains conditional on the policy and checker distribution used for calibration.

Written as a rule, let $\hat P_m$ be the calibrated estimate of the probability of an accepted result after $m$ units of admitted work, and $C_m$ the cumulative cost of that work. Marginal stopping halts when

$$
\frac{\hat P_m - \hat P_{m-1}}{C_m - C_{m-1}} < \epsilon_{\text{stop}},
$$ {#eq-vol3-marginal-stopping}

where $\epsilon_{\text{stop}}$ is the smallest gain in acceptance probability per unit cost that the task owner considers worth buying. In practice the runtime evaluates the ratio over a window of recent steps, because a single step's estimate is noisy. The threshold is an economic choice, not a property of the search: a task whose failure is expensive justifies a lower $\epsilon_{\text{stop}}$ than a task that can be retried cheaply.

The three stopping conditions apply in a fixed precedence. Hard ceilings on tokens, calls, depth, and elapsed time come first and hold unconditionally. Satisficing comes second: a candidate that meets the acceptance criteria ends search within those ceilings. The marginal rule of @eq-vol3-marginal-stopping comes last, deciding only whether to continue within what the first two leave open. Reversing the order would let an optimistic estimate override a mechanical limit, or let a flattening estimate stop a search that had already produced an acceptable candidate. @Fig-vol3-stopping-boundaries draws this precedence as the test the runtime applies before admitting more work.

::: {#fig-vol3-stopping-boundaries fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Stopping Precedence**: Before admitting more work, the runtime tests three conditions in a fixed order. A hard ceiling on tokens, calls, depth, or time stops search unconditionally. Within the ceilings, a candidate that meets the acceptance criteria ends search and goes to the acceptance decision, which stopping does not itself make. Only then does the marginal rule compare the gain per unit cost with $\epsilon_{\text{stop}}$. A stop without an acceptable candidate is reported as incomplete or escalated, never returned as accepted." fig-alt="Flowchart. A box reading before admitting more work leads to three diamonds in sequence: 1, hard ceiling reached; 2, acceptance criteria met; 3, gain per cost below epsilon stop. A no from the first two passes to the next diamond. A no from the third leads up to a box reading admit next work, which loops back to the start. Each yes leads down to an outcome card: stop unconditionally, listing tokens, calls, depth, and time and reading report incomplete, abstain, or escalate; stop search, reading return the candidate for the acceptance decision; and stop early, reading further work not worth its cost, report incomplete or escalate."}
![](images/svg/search_stopping_boundaries.svg)
:::

Benefit estimates guide how the runtime allocates the resources the hard limits leave and when it elects to stop early. When no useful continuation remains, the outcome still distinguishes an accepted deliverable from an unfinished candidate, and pending work stays in the ledger. The end of computation is not the end of the task.

::: {#chk-03-search-topologies .callout-checkpoint title="Accounting for a bounded search"}

The ledger and stopping policy must account for work even when it produces no accepted result.

- [ ] **Input budget**: Using the notebook's prompt length and expansion counts, can you estimate the input tokens spent on common prompts alone and explain why they exceed flat sampling's input count?
- [ ] **Pending work**: Which requests must remain reserved when the runtime reaches its deadline but remote cancellation is unconfirmed?
- [ ] **Stopping precedence**: A search has nearly exhausted its token ceiling, holds a candidate that passes the sealed suite, and still estimates a marginal gain above $\epsilon_{\text{stop}}$. Which rule decides, and what does the runtime do next?
- [ ] **Acceptance evidence**: What evidence would justify stopping with an accepted repair, and what should the runtime return if only the highest learned score is available?

:::

The search structure determines where the policy can spend work, while the ledger and stopping rules bound what it may spend and return. Which policy produces better accepted outcomes is settled by comparing complete policies under the same task conditions and resource ceilings, including the attempts that end without an accepted result.

## Deliberation Strategy Evaluation {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-strategy-design}

Suppose a new search policy repairs more connection-pool failures than the single-call baseline. The gain may come from better deliberation, or from a larger budget, a stronger underlying model, or silently discarded difficult cases. Evaluating a policy that combines allocation, selection, checks, and stopping therefore establishes what resources and permissions each policy receives, what it actually spends, and what happens to tasks for which no acceptable result arrives.

### Common limits, different expenditure

A controlled policy comparison holds the model, serving configuration, task set, available tools, and acceptance criteria fixed. It changes the deliberation policy while imposing common resource ceilings and a common deadline. Input tokens, generated tokens, check invocations, and allowed concurrency should be specified separately rather than collapsed into an ambiguous "compute budget." Policies need not consume their full allowances. Early stopping is part of the design, and unused allowance is not a measurement error.

A system-design comparison asks a different question. It may compare a stronger model used once with a smaller model used repeatedly, provided both operate within the same declared deployment constraints. Such a result describes the combined choice of model and policy; it cannot isolate the effect of deliberation alone. Keeping these questions separate prevents a model upgrade from being reported as a search improvement.

The evaluation must follow all assigned tasks, including failures and unfinished searches. Report final selected-output quality under an evaluator that is not merely the score optimized during search. Distinguish false acceptance from refusal or abstention, and distinguish both from running out of time. When reporting checker errors, state the denominator: the fraction of incorrect candidates that pass a check differs from the fraction of accepted outputs that are incorrect. Repeated trials should expose uncertainty and task-to-task variation rather than present a point estimate as a guarantee.

Actual expenditure includes unsuccessful branches, repeated input, selection, checks, and work still billed after cancellation. Dividing total cohort cost by the number of tasks meeting the stated acceptance criterion gives the cost per accepted task, the cohort form of $C_{\text{eff}}$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task); averaging only the costs of successful runs understates it by the failed attempts. Report latency distributions alongside this ratio, including the fraction completing within the deadline. A low average can hide a policy whose sequential revisions make its slowest tasks unusable.

### A deadline changes the policy

The following comparison uses a scoped test suite rather than an oracle for task truth. Its probabilities are stipulated inputs, not measurements or predictions about any particular model. The purpose is to show how concurrency and stopping change the work that a policy can actually complete.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-deliberation-strategy
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THREE HYPOTHETICAL POLICIES UNDER A COMMON DEADLINE (LEGO)
# │ Goal: Compare completed suite-pass opportunities and actual expenditure.
# │ Show: Deadline-censored probability, expected tokens/checks, time, and bill.
# │ How: Fixed round allowance; independent breadth; conditional feedback gain.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8
import math

class StrategyComparison:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    prompt = 2_048  # hypothetical fully serialized first request
    output = 1_000  # hypothetical generated tokens per candidate
    diagnostic = 340  # hypothetical failure-report tokens
    breadth = 8  # independent candidates, all generated and checked
    max_rounds = 3  # requested feedback cap, before deadline admission
    input_ceiling = 32_768
    output_ceiling = 8_192
    check_ceiling = 8
    concurrency = 8  # stipulated generator and check capacity
    deadline = 75 * second
    check_time = 10 * second  # distinct from earlier notebook scenarios
    initial_pass = 0.40  # scoped suite-pass probability for a fixed task
    revision_pass = 0.35  # conditional probability after a failed first attempt
    price_in = 3 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-input-token price
    price_out = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-output-token price

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / ureg.param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    round_time = output * token_time + check_time
    rounds = min(max_rounds, math.floor((deadline / round_time).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude))
    first_cost = prompt * price_in + output * price_out
    revision_input = prompt + output + diagnostic
    revision_cost = revision_input * price_in + output * price_out
    a_pass = initial_pass
    b_pass = 1 - (1 - initial_pass) ** breadth
    c_pass = initial_pass + (1 - initial_pass) * revision_pass
    c_rounds = 1 + (1 - initial_pass)
    a_input, b_input = prompt, breadth * prompt
    c_input = prompt + (1 - initial_pass) * revision_input
    a_output, b_output, c_output = output, breadth * output, c_rounds * output
    a_cost, b_cost = first_cost, breadth * first_cost
    c_cost = first_cost + (1 - initial_pass) * revision_cost
    c_time = c_rounds * round_time
    max_c_time = rounds * round_time
    requested_time = max_rounds * round_time
    a_bill_per_pass = a_cost / a_pass  # model bill per suite-passing task
    b_bill_per_pass = b_cost / b_pass
    c_bill_per_pass = c_cost / c_pass
    b_over_a = (b_bill_per_pass / a_bill_per_pass).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Validate Assumptions & Bounds) ─────────────────────────
    assert rounds == 2  # this notebook's conditional revision model has two rounds
    assert 0 <= initial_pass <= 1 and 0 <= revision_pass <= 1
    assert all(0 <= probability <= 1 for probability in (a_pass, b_pass, c_pass))
    assert max_c_time <= deadline < requested_time
    assert prompt > 0 and output > 0 and diagnostic >= 0
    assert round_time > 0 * second and check_time >= 0 * second
    assert breadth <= min(concurrency, check_ceiling)
    assert rounds <= check_ceiling
    assert max(b_input, prompt + revision_input) <= input_ceiling
    assert max(b_output, rounds * output) <= output_ceiling
    assert a_bill_per_pass < c_bill_per_pass < b_bill_per_pass

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Typed Prose Strings) ──────────────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    output_str = fmt_int(output)
    diagnostic_str = fmt_int(diagnostic)
    breadth_str = fmt_int(breadth)
    rounds_str = fmt_int(rounds)
    max_rounds_str = fmt_int(max_rounds)
    input_ceiling_str = fmt_int(input_ceiling)
    output_ceiling_str = fmt_int(output_ceiling)
    check_ceiling_str = fmt_int(check_ceiling)
    concurrency_str = fmt_int(concurrency)
    deadline_str = fmt_time(deadline, unit="s", precision=0)
    check_time_str = fmt_time(check_time, unit="s", precision=0)
    token_time_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit="ms", precision=3)
    round_time_str = fmt_time(round_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    requested_time_str = fmt_time(requested_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    max_c_time_str = fmt_time(max_c_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    c_time_str = fmt_time(c_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    initial_pass_str = fmt_percent(initial_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    revision_pass_str = fmt_percent(revision_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    b_pass_str = fmt_percent(b_pass, precision=2, style="prose")
    c_pass_str = fmt_percent(c_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    c_no_pass_str = fmt_percent(1 - c_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    c_rounds_str = fmt_ratio(c_rounds, precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    a_input_str, b_input_str, c_input_str = fmt_int(a_input), fmt_int(b_input), fmt_ratio(c_input, precision=1, commas=True)
    a_output_str, b_output_str, c_output_str = fmt_int(a_output), fmt_int(b_output), fmt_int(c_output)
    a_cost_str, b_cost_str, c_cost_str = fmt_usd(a_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(b_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(c_cost, precision=5)
    a_per_pass_str = fmt_int(a_output / a_pass)
    b_per_pass_str = fmt_int(b_output / b_pass)
    c_per_pass_str = fmt_int(c_output / c_pass)
    a_bill_per_pass_str = fmt_usd(a_bill_per_pass, precision=4)
    b_bill_per_pass_str = fmt_usd(b_bill_per_pass, precision=4)
    c_bill_per_pass_str = fmt_usd(c_bill_per_pass, precision=4)
    b_over_a_mult_str = fmt_multiple(b_over_a, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-03-strategy-comparison .callout-notebook title="Three policies, one deadline"}

**Scenario**: A repair task has a fixed, protected test suite. Each initial candidate passes it with hypothetical probability $p$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str`. Repeated runs concern the same task; breadth draws are independent conditional on that task. Passing this suite is the measured event, not proof that the repair meets every requirement. All policies receive the same tools and permissions, ceilings of `{python} StrategyComparison.input_ceiling_str` input tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.output_ceiling_str` generated tokens, and `{python} StrategyComparison.check_ceiling_str` tests, plus concurrency of `{python} StrategyComparison.concurrency_str` and a `{python} StrategyComparison.deadline_str` deadline.

Each initial request contains `{python} StrategyComparison.prompt_str` input tokens, and each candidate uses `{python} StrategyComparison.output_str` output tokens. Each test takes `{python} StrategyComparison.check_time_str`. Use the illustrative `{python} StrategyComparison.token_time_str` per-output-token allowance derived from the same registry inputs as @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost. Assume this allowance remains unchanged across concurrent streams and that all concurrent tests have dedicated capacity. Prefill, queueing, network, and selection overhead are omitted; this is not a service guarantee. Generation prices are hypothetical `{python} StrategyComparison.price_in_str` per million input tokens and `{python} StrategyComparison.price_out_str` per million output tokens, with no prefix discount.

**Option A (one candidate)**: Generate and test once. The suite-pass probability is `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str`; expenditure is `{python} StrategyComparison.a_input_str` input tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.a_output_str` output tokens, and one test. Completion takes `{python} StrategyComparison.round_time_str`, with a model bill of `{python} StrategyComparison.a_cost_str`. A failed test yields no accepted candidate.

**Option B (parallel breadth)**: Generate and test all `{python} StrategyComparison.breadth_str` independent candidates concurrently, without early cancellation. Select the first passing candidate in a predefined ordering, if any. The chance of an available suite-passing candidate is $1-(1-p)^k$, giving `{python} StrategyComparison.b_pass_str` here. Because selection uses the same binary suite outcome, that is also the probability of returning a suite-passing candidate. Completion takes `{python} StrategyComparison.round_time_str` under the concurrency assumption, but uses `{python} StrategyComparison.b_input_str` input tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.b_output_str` output tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.breadth_str` tests, and a model bill of `{python} StrategyComparison.b_cost_str`.

**Option C (feedback)**: Stop after the first pass; otherwise append the failed candidate and a `{python} StrategyComparison.diagnostic_str`-token diagnostic before requesting a revision. Conditional on the first failure, the revision has a hypothetical suite-pass probability $p_{\text{rev}}$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.revision_pass_str`. The requested cap is `{python} StrategyComparison.max_rounds_str` rounds, but those rounds would require `{python} StrategyComparison.requested_time_str`. Only `{python} StrategyComparison.rounds_str` complete rounds fit. The policy therefore admits at most one revision and stops after its check, with no accepted candidate if it fails.

**Math**: Feedback's deadline-censored pass probability is $p+(1-p)\,p_{\text{rev}}$, or `{python} StrategyComparison.c_pass_str`; its expected number of rounds is $1+(1-p)$, or `{python} StrategyComparison.c_rounds_str`. Expected expenditure is `{python} StrategyComparison.c_input_str` input tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.c_output_str` output tokens, and `{python} StrategyComparison.c_rounds_str` tests, with a model bill of `{python} StrategyComparison.c_cost_str`. Expected completion time is `{python} StrategyComparison.c_time_str`, and the maximum is `{python} StrategyComparison.max_c_time_str`. The remaining `{python} StrategyComparison.c_no_pass_str` of runs return no accepted candidate. They are budget-limited outcomes, not omitted trials or successful third attempts. Generated tokens per suite-passing task are about `{python} StrategyComparison.a_per_pass_str`, `{python} StrategyComparison.b_per_pass_str`, and `{python} StrategyComparison.c_per_pass_str` for A, B, and C, respectively.

**Systems insight**: Per suite-passing task, the model bill is `{python} StrategyComparison.a_bill_per_pass_str` for A, `{python} StrategyComparison.c_bill_per_pass_str` for C, and `{python} StrategyComparison.b_bill_per_pass_str` for B, `{python} StrategyComparison.b_over_a_mult_str` that of a single candidate. Feedback lifts the pass rate from `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str` to `{python} StrategyComparison.c_pass_str` for a small premium per success; breadth reaches `{python} StrategyComparison.b_pass_str` at the highest cost per success. The deadline is the knob that chooses between them: with room for only one `{python} StrategyComparison.round_time_str` round, breadth is the only way past `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str`; with room for two, feedback buys most of the gain cheaply; its third round, needing `{python} StrategyComparison.requested_time_str`, contributes nothing inside a `{python} StrategyComparison.deadline_str` deadline. Add each option's test count before comparing total cost per accepted task, and measure false acceptance separately, since a suite pass is not a repair.

:::

### Choosing an operating point

Each policy in the notebook wins on some metric. One candidate is cheapest, breadth has the highest stipulated suite-pass probability, and feedback offers an intermediate probability at intermediate expected expenditure but greater latency. A useful policy need not improve every metric over every simpler policy. A configuration is dominated only if another feasible configuration is at least as good on every chosen objective and strictly better on one. The remaining configurations offer trade-offs, from which the task's quality, risk, cost, and latency requirements determine an operating point.

This comparison also shows why probabilities must be calibrated under the deployed policy. Independent breadth draws do not justify substituting an informal "effective candidate count" into an exact probability formula. A revision's success probability is conditional on the failures and diagnostics that reach it. A deadline can remove later revisions from the deployed policy altogether. Held-out evaluation must preserve these conditions, including stopping behavior, rather than extrapolate an uncensored search curve into a constrained deployment.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-fallacies}

The common errors in deliberation design confuse additional work with the result that work is meant to improve, and each has a price that the chapter's own arithmetic makes visible.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *More generated tokens necessarily produce a better answer.*

Additional reasoning resolves implications of information already in the prompt, and it can just as easily elaborate a mistaken premise. When the open question is what the program does, generation is the slow way to find out: the `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str`-token explanation of @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-insufficient-response takes `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str`, `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str` the `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str` test that supplies the missing observation. Token count measures expenditure, not progress; keep extra reasoning only where its measured gain in selected-output quality justifies its latency.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating independent samples as independent capabilities.*

Draws that are independent for one task still share the model's blind spots across tasks, so pass@$k$ computed from a workload's average success rate overstates what a pool delivers (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity). A workload in which half the tasks pass at `{python} BestOfN.p_easy_str` and half never pass averages `{python} BestOfN.p_str`, the rate of notebook \ref{nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price}; substituting that average predicts `{python} BestOfN.naive_mix_str` for a pool of `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str`, while the true pool success is `{python} BestOfN.true_mix_str`, because no number of samples solves the tasks the model never solves. Compute pass@$k$ per task and average the results.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A check with a low false acceptance rate makes almost every pass trustworthy.*

Precision depends on the base rate of valid candidates as much as on the check (@eq-vol3-verifier-precision). With a `{python} CheckYield.eps_fa_str` false acceptance rate, a `{python} CheckYield.eps_fr_str` false rejection rate, and `{python} CheckYield.p_str` of candidates valid, only `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` of passing candidates are valid, and a first-pass selector returns a defective repair on `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str` of attempts (notebook \ref{nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under}). On hard tasks, the generator's valid rate is as much a lever on precision as the check itself.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Charging only for the final answer.*

Discarded candidates, repeated context, diagnostics, and selection all consume resources, and canceled requests may continue to incur cost. Parallel breadth in notebook \ref{nbk-03-strategy-comparison} returns one `{python} StrategyComparison.output_str`-token candidate but bills `{python} StrategyComparison.b_output_str` output tokens per task and `{python} StrategyComparison.b_per_pass_str` per suite-passing task; the beam in notebook \ref{nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs} reads `{python} SearchLedger.beam_prompt_tokens_str` input tokens to produce `{python} SearchLedger.beam_width_str` survivors for final testing. Charge the whole search, including unsuccessful tasks, to the cost per accepted task.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *The highest-scoring candidate has completed the task.*

A score orders candidates by one criterion, and argmax selection concentrates that criterion's errors in the winner: with Gaussian scoring noise, the selected candidate's expected error is about `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_large_str` standard deviations at `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates (@eq-vol3-argmax-noise), and a check gap present in `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_rate_str` of candidates appears in `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_present_str` of such pools. A top score supplies neither authority nor evidence for requirements the evaluator does not cover, and reaching the search limit leaves an unaccepted top scorer unaccepted.
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-ch3-summary}

Test-time compute turns one bounded model call into a bounded policy for allocating work. Depth, breadth, and feedback offer different opportunities to improve a candidate, but selection determines which candidate survives, and checks provide evidence only within their scope. Revisable plans preserve useful work by tracking the observations on which it depends. Resource accounting and stopping rules bound the resulting search without converting an unfinished or high-scoring proposal into an accepted result. The engineering decision is whether the deployed policy improves the required outcome enough to justify its actual expenditure and delay.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="More work needs a bounded policy"}

* **Allocation determines the shape of deliberation**: Depth adds sequential reasoning, breadth adds alternatives, and feedback conditions later attempts on observations. Their value depends on the task and selector; equal token allowances do not imply equal latency or equal quality.
* **Availability is not selected success**: A useful candidate can exist in the pool and still be discarded. Evaluate the generator and selector together, and distinguish a scoped check pass from evidence that the complete task has succeeded.
* **Checks have scope and error**: Accepted-set precision depends on candidate prevalence and checker behavior. Adaptive search can change both, so confidence measured on ordinary candidates need not survive optimization against the same score.
* **Revision must follow dependencies**: When relevant evidence or assumptions change, reconsider the candidate work that depends on them, not necessarily every earlier step. Reuse requires valid assumptions, and changing a plan does not undo actions already taken in the environment.
* **Limits change attainable outcomes**: A deadline removes unfinished branches and revisions from the policy's opportunities for success. Account for all expenditure, including failed tasks, and return an explicit unresolved outcome when no candidate meets the acceptance criteria.

:::

The deadline-censored comparison makes evidence-bounded deliberation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-test-time-scaling}) a property of the complete policy, not of candidate count alone. Its suite-pass probabilities also expose the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}): running a check and establishing that its verdict covers the task remain different obligations.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From deliberation to working state"}
Deliberation leaves candidate versions, failed hypotheses, observations, and dependency records. The next model call cannot treat all of them as equally current or useful. It needs a working context that retains the evidence supporting the selected candidate, distinguishes superseded material, and carries unresolved questions forward. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering develops this logical state-selection problem. Only after deciding what belongs in the working context does the physical question arise of how to store and reuse its model state, developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache.
:::

```{=latex}
\part{key:vol3_memory}
```
